Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task. Install the package, generate a key pair, open a UDP port, configure a peer, and connect a laptop. Within an afternoon, your staging environment can sit behind a private tunnel, and your internal dashboard can be restricted to traffic from a known address.

The initial setup is rarely the difficult part.

The real engineering work starts when the team changes. A developer joins, another leaves, someone replaces a laptop, a server needs patching, or a connection suddenly stops working. Each event creates a small maintenance task. Over time, those tasks become an operational responsibility that somebody must own.

This article examines what it takes to operate a self-hosted WireGuard VPN for a development team. We'll look at peer configuration, access management, troubleshooting, monitoring tools, and the engineering time involved. We'll also compare self-hosting with managed business VPN services so teams can make a decision based on their infrastructure needs.

WireGuard is a modern VPN protocol designed to establish encrypted connections between network peers. Its relatively small codebase, modern cryptography, and straightforward configuration make it attractive for developers who want control over their network infrastructure.

A basic WireGuard deployment typically involves:.

A server with a reachable public IP address.

A private and public key pair for the server.

A key pair for every client device.

A UDP port through which peers communicate.

Peer configuration that defines which addresses are allowed through the tunnel.

A simplified server configuration might look like this:.

The corresponding client configuration contains the client's private key and the server's public key:.

In a recent development, these examples illustrate the basic relationship between a server and a client. A production configuration will also need appropriate firewall rules, routing, DNS settings, and a blueprint for distributing configuration securely.

Recent findings suggest that the crucial distinction is that WireGuard establishes encrypted peer connections. It does not automatically provide a complete employee identity system, onboarding workflow, approval process, or audit dashboard.

Those responsibilities belong to the team operating the infrastructure.

Developers interested in using WireGuard on personal development devices can also explore SitePoint's guide to building a hardened mobile development environment with Termux, Docker, and WireGuard.

A peer is not just an entry in a configuration file. It represents a device that has permission to communicate through your network.

That makes peer management an access-control responsibility.

According to recent reports, for a small development team, it is tempting to keep a single configuration file and revision it manually whenever someone joins or leaves. This can work initially, but it becomes harder to manage as the number of devices increases.

A useful first step is to maintain a peer inventory:.

It has been revealed that the inventory should not contain private keys. Private keys must remain on their respective devices and should never be placed in a shared spreadsheet or source repository.

The inventory instead helps administrators answer practical questions:.

Which person owns this public key?

Which device is associated with this tunnel address?

Is the device still authorized?

When was its access last reviewed?

Has the peer been removed after the device was lost or replaced?

This information becomes especially notable when a team uses the VPN to reach staging servers, internal dashboards, databases, or other development resources.

Recent findings suggest that manual onboarding is manageable when a team has only two or three developers. It becomes unreliable when several people join, leave, or change devices over the year.

A repeatable onboarding process should cover more than generating a key pair.

A practical workflow looks like this:.

Confirm that the team member is authorized to access the environment.

Generate a key pair on the user's device.

Assign a unique tunnel address.

Add the public key to the server's peer configuration.

Apply the appropriate routing and firewall permissions.

Deliver the client configuration through a secure channel.

Test access to the specific development resources the person needs.

Record the peer owner, device, and approval details.

Offboarding needs an equally clear process:.

Identify every peer associated with the departing team member.

Remove the relevant public keys from the server.

Confirm that the configuration change has been applied.

Review any other credentials or allowlists that granted access.

Record when access was revoked.

An administrator can inspect the currently configured peers with:.

The output helps identify peer public keys, transfer counters, and latest handshake information. It is useful for troubleshooting, but it should not be treated as a complete access audit or proof that a particular person is still authorized.

The broader lesson is to make access changes part of a documented workflow. A peer should not remain active simply because nobody remembers who created it.

One common network-design mistake is assuming that connecting to a VPN should give a developer access to every internal service.

That is not necessarily the right model.

Sources indicate that A developer working on a frontend application may need access to a staging web server but not to the production database. A contractor may need access to one test environment without being able to reach internal administration tools.

WireGuard's peer configuration and the surrounding network controls should be designed around those requirements.

For example, teams can combine:.

Separate tunnel address ranges for different groups.

Firewall rules that restrict traffic to approved services.

Cloud security groups that limit access to specific ports.

Application-level authentication for internal dashboards.

Separate production and staging network boundaries.

The exact implementation depends on the infrastructure. The key point is that VPN membership and application authorization are different controls.

A successful VPN handshake should not be treated as permission to access every resource behind the tunnel.

Industry observers note that A VPN can appear simple when it works. Diagnosing it becomes more complicated when a developer is connecting from a home router, a hotel network, or a mobile hotspot.

DNS resolving to an unexpected address.

Incorrect routing or AllowedIPs settings.

Firewall rules blocking UDP traffic.

MTU problems that affect larger packets.

A peer using an outdated configuration.

A server process or host becoming unavailable.

WireGuard provides useful inspection commands:.

These commands help inspect peer information, check the service state, and review recent service logs. The exact systemd service name can differ depending on how the interface was configured.

Administrators should also monitor the underlying server. At minimum, that means checking:.

Whether the WireGuard interface is active.

Whether the UDP port is reachable.

Whether disk or memory usage is approaching a limit.

Whether operating-system and package updates are pending.

A small virtual server may be inexpensive, but it is still infrastructure that needs an owner.

Teams working with alternative tunnel-based development workflows may find SitePoint's tutorial on setting up Cloudflare Tunnels with Docker Compose for persistent webhook debugging useful. It covers a different tunneling use case, but the operational questions around connectivity, service health, and troubleshooting are closely related.

Sources indicate that A self-hosted VPN does not need to become a collection of manual tasks. A few established tools can make configuration, monitoring, and debugging more repeatable.

The core tool is, of course, WireGuard. Its command-line utilities allow administrators to inspect peers, manage interfaces, and review connection information. The official documentation is the best starting point for understanding configuration options and platform support.

Ansible can automate repeatable server administration tasks. A team could use playbooks to deploy configuration files, apply system updates, or standardize firewall settings across several VPN hosts.

It has been revealed that sensitive values should be handled with an appropriate secrets-management approach. Private keys should not be committed to a Git repository or stored in plaintext playbooks.

Prometheus is useful for collecting and querying metrics, while Node Exporter exposes Linux host metrics such as CPU, memory, disk, and network statistics.

According to recent reports, these tools do not automatically provide a complete WireGuard security audit. They can, however, help identify resource problems and server-health issues before those problems become user-reported outages.

Uptime Kuma provides a self-hosted monitoring dashboard with notifications. It can help teams monitor the availability of a VPN host or related services.

A basic availability check does not prove that every VPN peer can connect successfully. For more meaningful monitoring, combine host checks with an end-to-end test from a separate network.

Wireshark and tcpdump help developers inspect network traffic when diagnosing connectivity problems.

For example, tcpdump can capture UDP traffic on the WireGuard port:.

In a recent development, this can help determine whether packets are reaching the server. It does not decrypt WireGuard traffic or replace checks of routing, firewall rules, and peer configuration.

According to recent reports, the right toolset depends on the size of the deployment. A team with one VPN server may only need WireGuard's own commands and basic host monitoring. A larger environment may benefit from automation, centralized metrics, and a documented incident process.

It has been revealed that A self-hosted VPN can cost very little in direct infrastructure charges. However, the server invoice does not include the engineering time required to operate it.

Consider a hypothetical team with these assumptions:.

Two people join and two leave during the year.

The team reviews or rotates device keys quarterly.

Patching and monitoring require about two hours per month.

Six troubleshooting incidents occur annually.

The estimated loaded engineering cost is $60 per hour.

The virtual server costs approximately $6 per month.

The following estimate illustrates how quickly maintenance time can exceed the infrastructure bill.

At $60 per hour, 46 hours represent approximately $2,760 in engineering time. The server adds around $72 per year, bringing the estimated total to $2,832.

Sources indicate that these figures are illustrative, not a universal cost benchmark. A team with infrastructure automation and established monitoring may spend considerably less time. A team with frequent staff changes or strict audit requirements may spend more.

In a recent development, the useful exercise is to measure the work your own team performs. Track onboarding, access reviews, patching, incidents, and recovery time for a few months. That gives you a more realistic comparison than looking at hosting prices alone.

Self-hosting is not automatically the best option just because a team has developers who can configure servers.

A managed business VPN may be worth considering when the team needs centralized member management, simpler device administration, or a stable network exit address without maintaining the underlying VPN infrastructure.

Depending on the provider and strategy, managed services may offer:.

A central dashboard for adding and removing users.

Dedicated or shared IP options.

Client applications for common operating systems.

Multi-factor authentication or identity integrations.

Centralized administration and support.

For example, PureVPN for Teams is one service in this category. Teams evaluating it—or any other provider—should check the current feature set, pricing, logging practices, access controls, and service terms before making a decision.

A managed service does not remove every security responsibility. The team still needs to decide who receives access, review permissions, protect user accounts, and understand how traffic and metadata are handled.

Sources indicate that it also introduces vendor dependency and a recurring subscription cost. Those trade-offs should be considered alongside the engineering time saved.

There are situations where running WireGuard yourself is the more practical option.

You already operate infrastructure. If your team routinely patches servers, manages secrets, monitors services, and responds to incidents, maintaining a VPN may add relatively little work.

You need custom routing. A deployment that connects several private cloud networks, on-premises environments, or specialized subnets may require network controls that are easier to implement directly.

Sources indicate that you have strict data-control requirements. Some organizations have policies that limit which third parties can handle network traffic or related metadata. Those requirements may favor infrastructure under the organization's own control.

Industry observers note that you have a dedicated platform or security team. If someone is explicitly responsible for access management, monitoring, and incident response, self-hosting can fit naturally into existing operations.

Sources indicate that you can automate the lifecycle. Infrastructure-as-code, configuration management, documented peer inventories, and tested recovery procedures can reduce repetitive work and make a self-hosted deployment easier to maintain.

The vital distinction is between a deliberately operated service and a one-off server that nobody owns.

Before choosing an approach, ask the following questions:.

Who is responsible for the VPN six or twelve months after deployment?

How many people and devices are likely to join or leave?

How are public keys and peer configurations tracked?

How quickly can access be revoked when a device is lost?

Which internal services should each developer be able to reach?

Do you need a fixed egress IP for external allowlists?

What monitoring and recovery process exists if the server fails?

Do your customers or internal policies require access logs or formal reviews?

Does your team have the time and expertise to maintain the infrastructure?

Would a managed service cost less than the engineering time and operational risk it replaces?

If your team already has mature infrastructure practices and needs custom network control, self-hosting may be a sensible choice.

If the team is small, access changes frequently, and nobody has time to own another server, a managed service may be more practical.

WireGuard is an excellent protocol, and deploying it can be a straightforward engineering task. But operating a VPN for a development team involves more than establishing an encrypted connection.

Peer management, onboarding, offboarding, network permissions, monitoring, patching, and troubleshooting all require ongoing attention.

The right choice depends on the team's infrastructure experience, security requirements, size, and available engineering time. Self-hosting offers control and flexibility; a managed service can reduce operational work. Neither option removes the need for sound access-control practices.

Before deciding, calculate the maintenance effort, identify who will own the service, and make sure the design can be maintained as the team changes.

The cost example uses illustrative assumptions rather than current vendor pricing. Managed VPN features and prices can change, so verify provider details before purchasing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hugging Face AI Sheets is a new, open-source tool for building, enriching, and transforming datasets using AI models with no code. The tool can be deployed locally or on the Hub. It lets you use thousands of open models from the Hugging Face Hub via Inference Providers or local models, including gpt-oss from OpenAI!

Try the tool for free (no installation required): https://huggingface.co/spaces/aisheets/sheetsInstall and run locally: https://github.com/huggingface/sheets.

Industry observers note that AI Sheets is a no-code tool for building, transforming, and enriching datasets using (open) AI models. It’s tightly integrated with the Hub and the open-source AI ecosystem.

AI Sheets uses an easy-to-learn user interface, similar to a spreadsheet. The tool is built around quick experimentation, starting with small datasets before running long/costly data generation pipelines.

In AI Sheets, fresh columns are created by writing prompts, and you can iterate as many times as you need and edit the cells/validate cells to teach the model what you want. But more on this later!

Industry observers note that compare and vibe test models. Imagine you want to test the latest models on your data. You can import a dataset with prompts/questions, and create several columns (one per model) with a prompt like this: Answer the following: {{prompt}}, where prompt is a column in your dataset. You can validate the results manually or create a new column with an LLM as a judge prompt like this: Evaluate the responses to the following question: {{prompt}}. Response 1: {{model1}}. Response 2: {{model2}}, where model1 and model2 are columns in your dataset with different model responses.

It has been revealed that improve prompts for your data and specific models. Imagine you want to build an application to process customer requests and give automatic answers. You can load a sample dataset with customer requests and start playing and iterating with different prompts and models to generate responses. One cool feature of AI Sheets is that you can provide feedback by editing or validating cells. These example cells will be added to your prompts automatically. You can think of it as a tool to fine-tune prompts and add a few-shot examples to your prompts very efficiently, by looking at your data in real-time!

Sources indicate that transform a dataset. Imagine you want to clean up a column of your dataset. You can add a latest column with a prompt like Remove extra punctuation marks from the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to clean up.

Sources indicate that classify a dataset. Imagine you want to classify some content in your dataset. You can add a fresh column with a prompt like Categorize the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to categorize.

Analyze a dataset. Imagine you want to extract the main ideas in your dataset. You can add a new column with a prompt like this: Extract the most vital ideas from the following: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to analyze.

Enrich a dataset. Imagine you have a dataset with addresses that are missing zip codes. You can add a fresh column with a prompt like this: Find the zip code of the following address: {{address}} (in this case, you must enable the "Search the web" option to ensure accurate results).

Generate a synthetic dataset. Imagine you need a dataset with realistic emails, but the data is not available for data privacy reasons. You can create a dataset with a prompt like this: Write a short description of a professional in the field of pharma companies and name the column person_bio. Then you can create another column with a prompt like this Write a realistic professional email as it was written by the following person: {{person_bio}}.

Now let’s dive into how to use it!

It has been revealed that AI Sheets gives you two ways to start: import existing data or generate a dataset from scratch. Once your data is loaded, you can refine it by adding columns, editing cells, and regenerating content.

To get started, you need create one from scratch describing it in natural language or import an existing dataset.

Best for: Familiarizing with AI Sheets, brainstorming, rapid experiments, and creating test datasets.

Think of this as an auto-dataset or prompt-to-dataset feature—you describe what you want, and AI Sheets creates the entire dataset structure and content for you.

The following sections will show you how to iterate and expand the dataset.

This is recommended for most use cases, as importing real data gives you more control and flexibility than starting from scratch.

Pro tip: If your file contains minimal data, you can manually add more entries by typing directly into the spreadsheet.

Under the hood, these manually edited and liked cells will be used as few-shot examples for generating the cells when you regenerate or add more cells in the column!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities.
  • That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.
  • We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities. For example, Filipinos are among the most active ChatGPT people globally, ranking fourth in ChatGPT traffic (behind the United States, India, and Brazil [1] [2]), but despite this strong usage, we lack a clear understanding of how LLMs perform for their languages, such as Tagalog and Cebuano. Most of the existing evidence is anecdotal, such as screenshots of ChatGPT responding in Filipino as proof that it is fluent. What we need instead is a systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in Philippine languages.

That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.

We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.

According to recent reports, the FilBench evaluation suite contains four major categories–Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation–divided into 12 tasks. For example, the Classical NLP category includes tasks such as sentiment analysis, whereas Generation tasks include different aspects of translation. In order to ensure that these categories reflect the priorities and trends in NLP research and usage, we curate them based on a historical survey of NLP research on Philippine languages from 2006 to early 2024. (Most of these categories exclusively contain non-translated content to ensure faithfulness to the natural use of Philippine languages.).

Industry observers note that each of these categories provides an aggregated metric. To create a single representative score, we compute the weighted average based on the number of examples in each category, which we call the FilBench Score.

To simplify usage and set up, we built FilBench on top of Lighteval, an all-in-one framework for LLM evaluation. For language-specific evaluation, we first defined translation pairs from English to Tagalog (or Cebuano) for common terms used in evaluation such as "yes" (oo), "no" (hindi), and "true" (totoo) among others. Then, we used the provided templates to implement custom tasks for the capabilities we care about.

FilBench is now available as a set of community tasks in the official Lighteval repository!

By evaluating several LLMs on FilBench, we uncovered several insights into how they perform in Filipino.

According to recent reports, in the past few years, we have seen an increase in region-specific LLMs that target Southeast Asian languages (SEA-specific), such as SEA-LION and SeaLLM. These are open-weight LLMs that you can freely download from HuggingFace. We find that SEA-specific LLMs are often the most parameter-efficient for our languages, achieving the highest FilBench scores compared to other models of their size. However, the best SEA-specific model is still outperformed by closed-source LLMs like GPT-4o.

In a recent development, building region-specific LLMs still makes sense, as we observe performance gains of 2-3% when continuously fine-tuning a base LLM with SEA-specific instruction-tuning data. This suggests that efforts to curate Filipino/SEA-specific training data for fine-tuning remain relevant, as they can lead to better performance on FilBench.

According to recent reports, we also observe that across the four categories on FilBench, most models struggle with Generation capabilities. Upon inspecting failure modes in Generation, we find that these include cases where the model fails to follow translation instructions, generates overly verbose texts, or hallucinates another language instead of Tagalog or Cebuano.

The Philippines tends to have limited internet infrastructure and lower average incomes [3], necessitating accessible LLMs that are cost- and compute-efficient. Through FilBench, we were able to identify LLMs that are on the Pareto frontier of efficiency.

In general, we find that open-weight LLMs, i.e., models that you can freely download from HuggingFace, are way cheaper than commercial models without sacrificing their performance. If you want an alternative to GPT-4o for your Filipino language tasks, then try Llama 4 Maverick!

We also make this information available in the HuggingFace space of the FilBench leaderboard.

It has been revealed that we hope that FilBench provides deeper insights into LLM capabilities for Philippine languages and serves as a catalyst for advancing Filipino NLP research and development. The FilBench evaluation suite is built on top of Hugging Face's lighteval, allowing LLM developers to easily evaluate their models on our benchmark. For more information, please visit the links below:.

Industry observers note that the authors would like to thank Cohere Labs for providing credits through the Cohere Research Grant to run the Aya model series, and Together AI for additional computational credits for running several open models. We also acknowledge the Hugging Face team, particularly the OpenEvals team (Clémentine Fourrier and Nathan Habib) and Daniel van Strien, for their support in publishing this blog post.

If you are evaluating on FilBench, please cite our work:.

Tech Report: TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks.
  • Industry observers note that two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments.
  • Sources indicate that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

Industry observers note that two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

Sources indicate that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:.

Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step intends by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

According to recent reports, success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

For each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:.

According to recent reports, game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

In a recent development, harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

Long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel prepares as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

Industry observers note that dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is vital as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

It has been revealed that in closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai.

You can also plug them into MUDs (the few that still exist at least!) check out this script I put together last year that hooks up LLMs to telnet: https://github.com/CharlesCNorton/Language-Model-Tools/tree/main/AutoMUD.

With 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a upcoming kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

For the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

What makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

His work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

When shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

According to recent reports, "Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko says. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

The forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't new as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain consumers are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction.".

Khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The problem isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

Sources indicate that to understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

That translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

In a recent development, "The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko claims. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on.".

The result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

But the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

In a recent development, the difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

"Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko claims. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift.".

Executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

In a recent development, but Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he notes. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an vital and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it.".

What changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level users actually experience, is the profile that the upcoming workflow demands.

Khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

But this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he indicates. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible.".

Those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

According to recent reports, front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the new workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

In a recent development, separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

Sources indicate that shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

In a recent development, protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level customers actually experience.

Stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

Industry observers note that "The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko says. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests.".

In a recent development, the bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is presently visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.

Recent findings suggest that A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.

It has been revealed that nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.

China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.

The truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.

Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neural Super Sampling (NSS), a next-generation AI-powered upscaling solution from Arm is released for graphics and gaming developers to start experimenting today!

It has been revealed that NSS is designed for real-time performance on future mobile devices with Arm Neural Technology. However, latency depends on implementation factors such as GPU configuration, resolution, and use case. In our Enchanted Castle demo video below, NSS reduced GPU workload by 50 percent. The model rendered at 540p and upscaled to 1080p in just 4ms in sustained performance setup.

Recent findings suggest that neural Super Sampling (NSS) is a parameter prediction model for real-time temporal super sampling developed by Arm, optimized for execution on Neural Accelerators (NX) in mobile GPUs. It enables high-resolution rendering at a lower compute cost by reconstructing high-quality output frames from low-resolution temporal inputs. NSS is particularly suited for mobile gaming, XR, and other power-constrained graphics use cases.

Get started with our NSS model today.

If you want to go deeper check out the following resources:.

Check out the Neural Graphics Dataset: A collection of reference images and image sequences along with the corresponding motion, depth and other data required to train, validate and test neural super sampling algorithms.

The current version of the dataset includes a limited set of data for Neural Super Sampling to demonstrate how the NSS model development flow works. While this flow does not yet provide a comprehensive dataset for complete model (re)training, stay tuned for future releases of the Neural Graphics Model Gym where Arm will provide tools to capture and convert content for use in model training and retraining.

NSS has been integrated into Unreal Engine via two plugins, the NSS Plugin for Unreal® Engine and Unreal® NNE Plugin for ML extensions for Vulkan.

📅 13 Aug 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (904 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Arm & ExecuTorch 0.7: Bringing Generative AI to the masses

📅 13 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI.
  • Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack.
  • Sources indicate that when we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI. By embedding into widely-used Edge AI frameworks like XNNPack, MediaPipe, MNN, ONNX Runtime, and even llama.cpp, KleidiAI has delivered substantial performance improvements with no code changes required by developers. That foundation leads directly to the upcoming ExecuTorch 0.7 beta, where KleidiAI will be enabled by default—bringing automatic acceleration to devices built on the latest Arm CPU architecture, as well as a vast base of existing phones built on earlier generations.

Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack. The result? Faster model startups, lower latency, leaner memory footprints—and no integration hurdles. What previously required custom tuning is now turn-key performance, ready out of the box. This efficiency unlocks new possibilities—not just for the latest high-end devices, but for a much broader range of hardware.

Sources indicate that when we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. But what if we told you that GenAI experiences—like running large language models (LLMs)—can also be brought to devices that are 3, 4, or even 5 years old? Or even to the Raspberry Pi 5?

Well, this is no longer just a vision, but a practical reality. Thanks to the Arm SDOT CPU feature, which has been available in Arm CPUs since 2015.

The SDOT (Signed Dot Product) instruction, introduced in the Armv8.2 architecture and later CPUs, enables efficient dot product operations on vectors of 8-bit signed integers. The following image illustrates the behavior of one such SDOT instruction available on Arm CPUs:.

As shown above, the instruction produces four 32-bit integer outputs, each resulting from the dot product of corresponding groups of four int8 elements from the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) vector registers.

Sources indicate that this instruction can be utilized to accelerate matrix multiplication routines—the core computational workload behind every LLM—when using Int8 or lower-bit precision formats, such as Int4. These operations typically involve numerous dot products between individual rows of the left-hand side matrix and corresponding columns of the right-hand side matrix.

Recent findings suggest that the SDOT instruction is already widely supported across a diverse range of devices, opening the door for GenAI use cases to reach a significantly larger smartphone audience. As of today, Arm CPUs in approximately 3 billion Arm-based devices include this capability—enabling powerful on-device GenAI experiences for the majority of users. In fact, 72% of all devices now support this instruction.

Thanks to ExecuTorch, we are now enabling models like Llama 3.2 to run efficiently on the majority of Android devices as well as edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5.

Recent findings suggest that for the quantized Llama 3.2 1B announcement last year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams collaborated to deliver optimizations for the Int4 matrix-multiplication on Arm CPUs leveraging the I8MM feature, available from the Armv8.6 architecture onwards. As highlighted in a previous blog post, ExecuTorch with KleidiAI achieves over 20% higher prefill performance on the Galaxy S24+ compared to non-KleidiAI kernels.

Industry observers note that this translates to more than 350 tokens per second during the prefill phase and over 40 tokens per second during the decode phase. This level of performance is sufficient to enable on-device tasks, such as summarizing unread messages, with a smooth user experience using only Arm CPUs. For context, summarizing around 50 unread messages typically involves processing approximately 600 tokens.

This year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams have focused on optimizing Int4 matrix multiplication performance by leveraging the SDOT instruction, aiming to broaden adoption.

Check out the XNNPack PR on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that while LLM performance on Arm CPUs with only the SDOT extension may not match the latest flagship smartphones, it still enables impressive capabilities for on-device generative AI. In fact, in many scenarios, the decode phase is faster than the average human reading speed—highlighting that even older Arm CPUs can support practical and meaningful GenAI use cases.

For example, when combined with speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, a local LLM of this kind enables the creation of a fully private smart assistant that operates entirely offline, eliminating concerns about data privacy while still offering rich voice-based interactions. Such a device could seamlessly interact with your connected devices, ensuring users have peace of mind with their data.

In a recent development, another compelling use case for running Llama 3.2 1B is context-aware text completion in local text editors. As you type, the model provides intelligent, real-time suggestions to streamline writing or coding workflows—all without requiring an internet connection.

These are just a few examples, and they only scratch the surface of what is possible with on-device GenAI.

It has been revealed that with the combined power of SDOT, KleidiAI, and ExecuTorch, we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Bringing Generative AI beyond high-end flagship devices and making it accessible on billions of Arm-based devices already in use.

Recent findings suggest that now it is your turn—we are excited to see what you will create. To help you get started, check out Arm’s learning path, designed to guide you through developing your own applications with LLMs using ExecuTorch and KleidiAI.

Build an Android chat app with Llama, KleidiAI, ExecuTorch, and XNNPACK.

Breaking: SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20%

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years.
  • The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month.
  • SED claims that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a fresh report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED claims that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far.".

According to recent reports, those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Sources indicate that another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

It has been revealed that but according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

In a recent development, on net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

Tech Report: Kimina-Prover-RL

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.
  • We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.
  • This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.

We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.

This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.

It is released as part of a fork of Verl containing the complete training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, allowing anyone to reproduce our experiments or adapt the setup to their own models and datasets. All information to setup and launch the pipeline can be found in the README of the recipe.

As a result of this training pipeline, we are releasing two models:.

kimina-prover-rl is a training pipeline designed to teach large language models to solve formal proof goals in Lean 4, using a two-stage output structure: a natural language reasoning trace followed by corresponding Lean code.

This paradigm, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, enables the model to separate planning from execution, promoting explainability, error recovery, and stronger generalization.

To train models under this reasoning framework, we apply GRPO — a reinforcement learning approach tailored for LLMs. This open-source version of the training pipeline of Kimina-prover is implemented using the RL library Verl.

During the rollout phase of GRPO, the model generates N outputs for each prompt. A reward of 1 is assigned to any output whose Lean code is successfully verified by Lean using our kimina-lean-server.

Two main features are added to this framework:.

During training, a large number of Lean 4 proof candidates must be verified simultaneously. To handle this efficiently, we require a high-throughput verification system.

To meet this need, Numina and Kimi have developed an open-source server called kimina-lean-server, which supports parallel proof checking at scale using Lean 4.

To simplify integration, we also provide kimina-client, a lightweight Python package (available on PyPI) that offers a clean interface for interacting with the server’s API.

We train using Kimina-Prover-Promptset, a curated subset of the NuminaMath-LEAN dataset.

For this training setup, we filter and preprocess the dataset as follows:.

The resulting dataset contains challenging, high-value problems for improving Lean 4 theorem proving models.

NuminaMath-LEAN-RL is also the dataset used to train AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B and AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-0.6B.

The core idea of our reasoning training pipeline is to structure the LLM output into two stages. One thinking block followed by one lean4 block:.

According to recent reports, each rollout is verified to ensure that this format is respected. If the output is malformed — e.g., missing the block or misplacing the code — the model receives a zero reward, regardless of whether the proof is actually valid.

This enforces consistency and teaches the model to structure its outputs reliably.

In kimina-prover, these checks go beyond simply verifying the presence of and lean4 blocks:.

Only generations that pass all these checks are considered well-formatted and can receive a reward. This structured filtering improves training stability and encourages clean reasoning.

To make training more informative, we have added an error correction mechanism that gives the model a chance to fix its own failed proofs.

When a rollout fails (e.g., due to a Lean error or incorrect proof), we:.

This encourages the model to learn from failure signals as lean feedback is provided during the training.

It also enables multi-turn interaction chains, where feedback from Lean is injected as part of the prompt, and the model is rewarded for successfully debugging its own output.

Because multi-turn responses can get long, we allow only one error-fix turn and cap the error message at a set number of tokens.

The work Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective claims there's optimization bias in GRPO, that leads to artificially longer responses, especially for incorrect outputs.

We also noticed this behaviour during our experimentations and we used DrGPO for our optimization. DrGRPO aggregates token-level losses by normalizing with a global constant to eliminate length bias.

The configuration file provided in the repository is for a 8 GPUs setup.

It has been revealed that the model that we are finetunning is the AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-Distill-1.7B. This model is a finetuned version of Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B with cold start data generated from our AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-72B model.

At every step, 256 samples are fetched in the training dataset. One out of two is an error correction sample. We generate 8 rollout per samples so 2048 generations. You can increase to 16 or 32 rollouts if you are using more than one node.

In a recent development, we evaluate the model every 5 training steps, using the best@8 metric from verl to have fast validation steps. You can increase to best@16 or 32 if you are using more than one node. We are evaluating the performance before and the after the error correction turn. For each failed reponse we allow the model to do one more tentative to fix its proof.

Industry observers note that after a few training steps, we observe a consistent improvement in performance. In this section we will discuss the training metrics after 48 hours of training on 8 H100 GPUs.

By step 85, the pipeline improves the model's accuracy by 4 points, reaching 70% for the best@8 metric and 74% after the error correction turn:.

In parallel, we observe that the number of format errors steadily decreases over the course of training, indicating that the model is learning to produce structurally valid outputs.

Finally, and as expected under the DeepSeek-R1-style training setup, the average token length of the model’s outputs increases with training — a signal that the model is learning to reason in longer, more structured traces.

According to recent reports, after the training, we evaluated the model using pass@32 with and without error fixing. We were able to improve the performances of our 1.7B model by more than 3% at pass@32 on MiniF2F:.

Using this training pipeline we also finetuned a 0.6B model, improving its performances by more than 2%.

With Kimina-Prover-RL, we provide a lightweight yet powerful reinforcement learning pipeline for training Lean 4 theorem provers.

By combining structured reasoning, format rewards, and error correction, we achieve state-of-the-art results for open-source models in the 0.6B–1.7B parameter range.

Alongside the models, we are also releasing a fork of Verl containing the full training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, so the community can reproduce our results or adapt the pipeline to their own datasets and models.

We hope this release will serve as a solid foundation for the community to experiment with RL training in formal reasoning, and to push the limits of open-source automated theorem proving in Lean 4.

Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today.
  • Industry observers note that there are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat.
  • These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

Industry observers note that there are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi highlights casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA claims that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists released Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

Industry observers note that in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

In a recent development, the decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

According to recent reports, NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

Recent findings suggest that however, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

In a recent development, in our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

According to recent reports, this does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

In our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

Industry observers note that kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The crucial point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

Removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

The resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

Sources indicate that that distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Sources indicate that our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

Other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

In a recent development, A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

Sources indicate that NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address blueprint, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not key.

According to recent reports, an overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Recent findings suggest that direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are crucial. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

The broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

According to recent reports, as more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

In a recent development, sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

If most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.
