Academic research involves frequent research discovery: finding papers, code, related models and datasets. This typically means switching between platforms like arXiv, GitHub, and Hugging Face, manually piecing together connections.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that allows agentic models to communicate with external tools and data sources. For research discovery, this means AI can use research tools through natural language requests, automating platform switching and cross-referencing.

Much like software development, research discovery can be framed in terms of layers of abstraction.

At the lowest level of abstraction, researchers search manually and cross-reference by hand.

Industry observers note that this manual approach becomes inefficient when tracking multiple research threads or conducting systematic literature reviews. The repetitive nature of searching across platforms, extracting metadata, and cross-referencing information naturally leads to automation through scripting.

Python scripts automate research discovery by handling web requests, parsing responses, and organizing results.

The research tracker demonstrates systematic research discovery built from these types of scripts.

According to recent reports, while scripts are faster than manual research, they often fail to automatically collect data due to changing APIs, rate limits, or parsing errors. Without human oversight, scripts may miss relevant results or return incomplete information.

MCP makes these same Python tools accessible to AI systems through natural language.

The AI orchestrates multiple tools, fills information gaps, and reasons about results:.

This can be viewed as an additional layer of abstraction above scripting, where the "programming language" is natural language. This follows the Software 3.0 Analogy, where the natural language research direction is the software implementation.

This comes with the same caveats as scripting:.

The easiest way to add the Research Tracker MCP is through Hugging Face MCP Settings:.

According to recent reports, this workflow leverages the Hugging Face MCP server, which is the standard way to use Hugging Face Spaces as MCP tools. The settings page provides client-specific configuration that's automatically generated and always up-to-date.

Ready to automate your research discovery? Try the Research Tracker MCP or build your own research tools with the resources above.

Custom CUDA kernels give your models a serious performance edge, but building them for the real world can feel daunting. How do you move beyond a simple GPU function to create a robust, scalable system without getting bogged down by endless build times and dependency nightmares?

We created the kernel-builder library for this purpose. You can develop a custom kernel locally, and then build it for multiple architectures and make it available for the world to use.

In this guide we'll show you how to build a complete, modern CUDA kernel from the ground up. Then, we’ll tackle the tough production and deployment challenges, drawing on real-world engineering strategies to show you how to build systems that are not just fast, but also efficient and maintainable.

When you're done, other developers will be able to use your kernels directly from the hub like this:.

According to recent reports, let's build a practical kernel that converts an image from RGB to grayscale. This example uses PyTorch's modern C++ API to register our function as a first-class, native operator.

In a recent development, A clean, predictable structure is the foundation of a good project. The Hugging Face Kernel Builder expects your files to be organized like this:.

Industry observers note that this file orchestrates the entire build. It tells the kernel-builder what to compile and how everything connects.

To ensure anyone can build your kernel on any machine, we use a flake.nix file. It locks the exact version of the kernel-builder and its dependencies, eliminating "it works on my machine" complications.

Sources indicate that now for the GPU code. Inside csrc/img2gray.cu, we'll define a kernel that uses a 2D grid of threads—a natural and efficient fit for processing images.

This is the most crucial step. We're not just binding to Python; we're registering our function as a native PyTorch operator. This makes it a first-class citizen in the PyTorch ecosystem, visible under the torch.ops namespace.

The file torch-ext/torch_binding.cpp handles this registration.

In simple terms, TORCH_LIBRARY_EXPAND allows us to define our operator in a way that can be easily extended or modified in the future.

This approach is crucial for two main reasons:.

It has been revealed that compatibility with torch.compile: By registering our kernel this way, torch.compile can "see" it. This allows PyTorch to fuse your custom operator into larger computation graphs, minimizing overhead and maximizing performance. It's the key to making your custom code work seamlessly with PyTorch's broader performance ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that hardware-Specific Implementations: This system allows you to provide different backends for the same operator. You could add another TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(img2gray, CPU, ...) block pointing to a C++ CPU function. PyTorch's dispatcher would then automatically call the correct implementation (CUDA or CPU) based on the input tensor's device, making your code powerful and portable.

Setting up the __init__.py wrapper.

In torch-ext/img2gray/ we need an __init__.py file to make this directory a Python package and to expose our custom operator in a user-friendly way.

The _ops module is auto-generated by kernel-builder from a template to provide a standard namespace for your registered C++ functions.

You can build your kernel with a single command, nix build . -L; however, as developers, we'll want a faster, more iterative workflow. For that, we'll use the nix develop command to enter a development shell with all the necessary dependencies pre-installed.

This command creates a handful of files used to build the kernel: CMakeLists.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py, and a cmake directory. The CMakeLists.txt file is the main entry point for CMake to build the kernel.

Now you can install the kernel in editable mode.

🙌 Amazing! We now have a custom built kernel that follows best practices for PyTorch bindings, with a fully reproducible build process.

To ensure everything is working correctly, we can run a simple test to check that the kernel is registered and it works as expected. If it doesn't, you can iterate by editing the source files and repeating the build, reusing the nix environment you created.

Now that we have a working kernel, it's time to share it with other developers and the world!

One small thing we'll want to do before we share, is clean up all of the development artifacts that were generated during the build process to avoid uploading unnecessary files.

Earlier, we built the kernel for a specific version of PyTorch and CUDA. However, to make it available to a wider audience, we need to build it for all supported versions. The kernel-builder tool can help us with that.

This is also where the concept of a compliant kernel comes into play. A compliant kernel is one that can be built and run for all supported versions of PyTorch and CUDA. Generally, this requires custom configuration; however, in our case, the kernel-builder tool will automate the process.

This process may take a while, as it will build the kernel for all supported versions of PyTorch and CUDA. The output will be in the result directory.

The kernel-builder team actively maintains the supported build variants, keeping them current with the latest PyTorch and CUDA releases while also supporting trailing versions for broader compatibility.

The last step is to move the results into the expected build directory (this is where the kernels library will look for them).

In a recent development, once you have a ready-to-use kernel, there are some things you can do to make it easier to deploy your kernel. We will discuss using versioning as a tool to make API changes without breaking downstream use of kernels. After that, we will wrap up showing how you can make Python wheels for your kernel.

You might decide to update your kernel after a while. Maybe you have found new ways of improving performance or perhaps you would like to extend the kernel's functionality. Some changes will require you to change the API of your kernel. For instance, a newer version might add a new mandatory argument to one of the public functions. This can be inconvenient to downstream users, because their code would break until they add this new argument.

A downstream user of a kernel can avoid such breakage by pinning the kernel that they use to a particular revision. For instance, since each Hub repository is also a Git repository, they could use a git commit shorthash to pin the kernel to a revision:.

Using a Git shorthash will reduce the chance of breakage; however, it is hard to interpret and does not allow graceful upgrades within a version range. We therefore recommend using the familiar semantic versioning system for Hub kernels. Adding a version to a kernel is easy: you simply add a Git tag of the form vx.y.z where x.y.z is the version. For instance, if the current version of the kernel is 1.1.2, you can tag it as v1.1.2. You can then get that version with get_kernel:.

Industry observers note that versioning becomes even more powerful with version bounds. In semantic versioning, the version 1.y.z, must not have backward-incompatible changes in the public API for each succeeding x and y. So, if the kernel's version was 1.1.2 at the time of writing your code, you can ask the version to be at least 1.1.2, but less than 2.0.0:.

This will ensure that the code will always fetch the latest kernel from the 1.y.z series. The version bound can be a Python-style version specifier.

You can tag a version with huggingface-cli:.

In large projects, you may want to coordinate the kernel versions globally rather than in each get_kernel call. Moreover, it is often useful to lock kernels, so that all your consumers have the same kernel versions, which aids handling bug reports.

According to recent reports, the kernels library offers a nice way of managing kernels at the project-level. To do so, add the kernels package to the build-system requirements of your project, in the pyproject.toml file. After doing so, you can specify your project's kernel requirements in the tools.kernels section:.

Recent findings suggest that the version can be specified with the same type of version specifiers as Python dependencies. This is another place where the version tags (va.b.c) come handy -- kernels will use a repository's version tags to query what versions are available. After specifying a kernel in pyproject.toml, you can lock it to a specific version using the kernels command-line utility. This utility is part of the kernels Python package:.

Recent findings suggest that this generates a kernels.lock file with the latest kernel versions that are compatible with the bounds that are specified in pyproject.toml. kernels.lock should be committed to your project's Git repository, so that every user of the project will get the locked kernel versions. When newer kernels versions are released, you can run kernels lock again to update the lock file.

You need one last bit to fully implement locked kernels in a project. The get_locked_kernel is the counterpart to get_kernel that uses locked kernels. So to use locked kernels, replace every occurrence of get_kernel with get_locked_kernel:.

That's it! Every call of get_locked_kernel("drbh/img2gray") in the project will now use the version specified in kernels.lock.

According to recent reports, the get_locked_kernel function will download the kernel when it is not available in the local Hub cache. This is not ideal for applications where you do not want to download binaries at runtime. For example, when you are building a Docker image for an application, you usually want the kernels to be stored in the image along with the application. This can be done in two simple steps.

First, use the load_kernel function in place of get_locked_kernel:.

According to recent reports, as the name suggests, this function will only load a kernel, it will never try to download the kernel from the Hub. load_kernel will raise an exception if the kernel is not locally available. So, how do you make the kernels locally available? The kernels utility has you covered! Running kernels download . will download the kernels that are specified in kernels.lock. So e.g. in a Docker container you could add a step:.

and the kernels will get baked into your Docker image.

Kernels use the standard Hugging Face cache, so all HF_HOME caching rules apply.

We strongly recommend downloading kernels from the Hub using the kernels package. This has many benefits:.

You’ve seen how to build a custom kernel from the ground up, register it as a native PyTorch operator, and share it with the community on the Hugging Face Hub. In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the firm plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the organization’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

In a recent development, for years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has revealed it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the firm describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:.

It has been revealed that while flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

In a recent development, google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

According to recent reports, back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Sources indicate that A new device on Kickstarter claims to make Game Boy cartridges relevant again by playing soundtracks from your favorite classic Nintendo games. The Retro Song Bird is a box-shaped speaker that supports Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with support for over 1,900 games. Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

Recent findings suggest that the Retro Song Bird also comes with a 3.5mm stereo line-out and a USB Type-C port in case you want to connect to other audio equipment. According to the developer, it offers accurate, register-level sound emulation and can be used to sample and remix music from your Game Boy cartridges. It exposes all four audio channels (two square, wave, noise) as separate USB audio streams that can be imported into a DAW. This allows you to isolate individual melodies, waveforms, and sound effects from old games to create your own melodies. There’s even support for LSDj for playing saved chiptune tracks, while two Retro Song Bird units can be synced for DJ-style performances using Game Boy cartridges instead of traditional records.

In addition to playing retro video game soundtracks, the Retro Song Bird also supports the Game Boy Camera, allowing you to use it as a webcam offering a glorious 128×112 pixels resolution and 5 frames per second speed. Other features include the ability to back up and restore save files, ROMs, flash writable carts, and export any soundtrack or sound effect as WAV onto your PC. The listing also includes other abilities, including an Alarm Mode, a record of every cartridge you've ever plugged in, an open API for developers, and over-the-air updates.

The Retro Song Bird is currently available to back on Kickstarter, with the standard model starting at $79. The introductory $59 Early Bird offer has already sold out, while the developer is also offering a two-unit bundle for $150. Shipments are expected to begin in April 2027.

According to recent reports, the developer notes that only a handful of hand-assembled prototypes currently exist and that the hardware and design still need some refinements. The project also faces potential manufacturing challenges, including component availability, finding suitable manufacturing partners, and producing injection-molded enclosures. Like any other Kickstarter campaign, delivery timelines are subject to change, and backers should be aware that there is no guarantee the finished product will ship as planned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and promptly switch devices on the fly.

Sources indicate that other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”.

In a recent development, there are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier.

Recent findings suggest that as per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Industry observers note that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

According to recent reports, the best accounts receivable software for your company is the layer that closes the stage where your cash leaks. If buyers settle from an emailed link and outreach starts late, a reminders tool covers most of it. If customers prefer to pay online by card or ACH, add a payments network with a customer portal. If clients require invoice uploads to Coupa or Ariba and clear multiple invoices with one blank-memo wire, you need an AR automation layer on top of the ERP. Every platform listed here serves B2B businesses invoicing other companies, excluding consumer payment apps and collection agencies.

Our source material is each vendor's public product, integration, security and pricing pages, plus G2 reviews, as they stood in November 2026.

In a recent development, about three in five US suppliers let business clients pay within 30 days, per Atradius's 2026 US payment practices survey (September 2026). Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:.

What invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

The ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

On Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

Portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

Industry observers note that to say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the firm’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

It has been revealed that we’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe states that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit.

But the question at this point is, do you even like this fresh look?

Sources indicate that personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago.
  • It has been revealed that "Our momentum is real.
  • For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set latest financial records as demand for its AI accelerators indicates no signs of slowing down. The organization reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.

It has been revealed that "Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," mentioned Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.".

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The manufacturer's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.

As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the company's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.

One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The firm also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.

Sources indicate that "Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028.".

To support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The manufacturer's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that the company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.

It has been revealed that the commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday revealed new partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the tech giant disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.

According to recent reports, during the earnings call, Kress said that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the manufacturer to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.

According to recent reports, although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The company raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.

It has been revealed that in addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the company's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.

In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.

Nvidia currently absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the company expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.

Going forward, Nvidia plans to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the manufacturer expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.

"We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress said. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a new pricing, as we moved into the new year.".

Sources indicate that perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.

Sources indicate that for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The company expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress stated that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

To best take advantage of English knowledge instilled during pre‑training, we translate the user prompt and model response while preserving the original English reasoning chain.

#57839. XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2359 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we?
  • XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space.
  • There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through massive ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space. The manufacturer has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

But first, let’s talk hardware.

XREAL Aura is a two-part device. There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing. It’s wildly different from a typical VR headset, while also having most of the same benefits. Unlike most other XREAL glasses, Aura has built-in world-facing cameras used for hand and spatial tracking, as well as being able to be used as a camera for things like scanning QR codes, Gemini Live, or simply taking a quick picture (there’s no privacy light here, but the bulkier-than-normal design compared to standard glasses is more than enough a dead giveaway that the “perv glasses” dilemma doesn’t really apply in my opinion).

The other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

Industry observers note that together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

It has been revealed that where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

And that brings us to Android XR.

In a recent development, google’s platform launched on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor demonstrates where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

Some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

In a recent development, like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as significant as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

In a recent development, there’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers promptly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

Recent findings suggest that performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

But how do you actually use a product like this?

That’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

Both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

It has been revealed that by far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any significant movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab shows promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

It has been revealed that the other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

In a recent development, XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

Further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

Sources indicate that we’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of massive problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

Don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that even though Nvidia states that it does not plan to bring its former CEO Jensen Huang back to the company, that hasn't stopped some of its board members from continuing to lobby for his return. Following the news that some of Huang's allies have formed a "war room" to drive his reinstatement just days after his resignation, one Nvidia employee went so far as to warn that the company faces the possibility of an exodus of "irreplaceable talent" if Huang isn't reinstated. We've even seen U.S. President Trump argue for giving Huang his old job back, but the company stated during its November 17 earnings call that wasn't in the cards. Now, Semafor reports that some Nvidia board members aren't taking "no" for an answer.

Industry observers note that huang, for his part, has already stated that he would be "honored" to return to the company that he resigned from in disgrace just a few days ago. At the time, he admitted to having an affair with a woman who worked for Megaspeed, a controversial Nvidia customer linked to the smuggling of export-controlled AI hardware into China. That woman has also been accused of being a Chinese spy, further complicating an already troublesome matter for Nvidia and Huang. Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer will make an appearance before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees in early December and are likely to face some difficult questions.

But despite all of this, Huang is stated to have spoken with at least one Nvidia board member about the possibility of making a return to Nvidia. That meeting took place hours before Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the firm’s earnings call that Huang wasn't coming back. The board voted unanimously to accept his resignation, and won't be backtracking. It's reported that three board members don't agree with that stance, while others have already turned their attention to who will replace Huang long-term. Interim CEO Colette Kress is not being considered as a full-time replacement for Huang.

Instead, Arm CEO Rene Haas has appeared as a frontrunner for the top job, with the Nvidia board believed to have already made an approach. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy is also another name under consideration, but the ongoing calls for Huang to be brought back into the fold are thought to have put him off. Rene Haas has reportedly been considere.

It isn't just some of Nvidia's board members who have rallied around Huang. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney have also chimed in, while a Taiwanese skyscraper was used to send messages of support to a man who has proven hugely popular in the country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most Chinese-brand Android phones don’t like it when you use a 3rd-party launcher, but the ColorOS 17 upgrade may be changing that.

Recent findings suggest that if I hop on a phone from Oppo, Vivo, Honor, or most other Chinese brands and try to use a 3rd-party launcher, I’m definitely not going to like how the phone operates. Often, there’s a weird delay when navigating back home or opening the Overview multitasking screen. Sometimes, Overview doesn’t work at all, essentially forcing you back to the default launcher that shipped with the phone.

Industry observers note that but one Reddit user says Oppo is doing things differently in the ColorOS 17 update. According to their experience, the delay and other issues with 3rd-party launchers are completely solved. OnePlus’s OxygenOS doesn’t have the same issues, so it’s good to see that OnePlus users who are still set to receive ColorOS 17 in the near future won’t feel like their phones are losing a valuable feature.

Chinese Android brands like Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Realme, and several others often outshine Western brands in many ways, but they’ve always had one annoying weakness: software. Whether it’s the number of updates a phone receives, overall quality, or another specific issue, Chinese brands often build very different visions of Android than Google, Samsung, Motorola, or Nothing.

The value and hardware prowess these phones usually deliver help outshine software weaknesses, and these companies have been steadily improving software over the past year or two to meet the demands of a more Westernized audience. Companies like Honor now offer 7 years of software updates, and ColorOS is widely regarded as the best Android skin next to Samsung’s One UI in many circles. That’s great news for everyone, especially in an age where fewer smartphone companies compete for your hard-earned dollars.

Make your ZeroGPU Spaces go brrr with ahead-of-time compilation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic.
  • Industry observers note that this is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in.
  • The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ZeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic. It’s efficient, flexible, and ideal for demos but it doesn’t always make full use of everything the GPU and CUDA stack can offer. Generating images or videos can take a significant amount of time. Being able to squeeze out more performance, taking advantage of the H200 hardware, does matter in this case.

Industry observers note that this is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in. Instead of compiling models on the fly (which doesn’t play nicely with ZeroGPU’s short-lived processes), AoT lets you optimize once and reload instantly.

The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.

Industry observers note that in this post, we’ll show how to wire up Ahead-of-Time (AoT) compilation in ZeroGPU Spaces. We'll explore advanced tricks like FP8 quantization and dynamic shapes, and share working demos you can try right away. If you cannot wait, we invite you to check out some ZeroGPU-powered demos on the zerogpu-aoti organization.

Pro customers and Team / Enterprise org members can create ZeroGPU Spaces, while anyone can freely use them (Pro, Team and Enterprise users get 8x more ZeroGPU quota).

Spaces is a platform powered by Hugging Face that allows ML practitioners to easily publish demo apps.

Typical demo apps on Spaces look like:.

This works great, but ends up reserving a GPU for the Space during its entire lifetime – even when it has no user activity.

When executing .to('cuda') on this line:.

In a recent development, pyTorch initializes the NVIDIA driver, which sets up the process on CUDA forever. This is not very resource-efficient given that app traffic is not perfectly smooth, but is rather extremely sparse and spiky.

ZeroGPU takes a just-in-time approach to GPU initialization. Instead of setting up the main process on CUDA, it automatically forks the process, sets it up on CUDA, runs the GPU tasks, and finally kills the fork when the GPU needs to be released.

Thanks to the Python spaces package, the only code change needed to get this behaviour is as follows:.

By importing spaces and adding the @spaces.GPU decorator, we:.

ZeroGPU currently allocates an MIG slice of H200 (3g.71gb profile). Additional MIG sizes including full slice (7g.141gb profile) will come in late 2025.

It has been revealed that modern ML frameworks like PyTorch and JAX have the concept of compilation that can be used to optimize model latency or inference time. Behind the scenes, compilation applies a series of (often hardware-dependent) optimization steps such as operator fusion, constant folding, etc.

PyTorch (from 2.0 onwards) at the moment has two major interfaces for compilation:.

torch.compile works great in standard environments: it compiles your model the first time it runs, and reuses the optimized version for subsequent calls.

Industry observers note that however, on ZeroGPU, given that the process is freshly spun up for (almost) every GPU task, it means that torch.compile can’t efficiently re-use compilation and is thus forced to rely on its filesystem cache to restore compiled models. Depending on the model being compiled, this process takes from a few dozen seconds to a couple of minutes, which is way too much for practical GPU tasks in Spaces.

This is where ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation shines.

Industry observers note that with AoT, we can export a compiled model once, save it, and later reload it instantly in any process, which is exactly what we need for ZeroGPU. This helps us reduce framework overhead and also eliminates cold-start timings typically incurred in just-in-time compilation.

Sources indicate that but how can we do ahead-of-time compilation on ZeroGPU? Let’s dive in.

It has been revealed that let's go back to our ZeroGPU base example and unpack what we need to enable AoT compilation. For the purpose of this demo, we will use the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev model:.

In the discussion below, we only compile the transformer component of pipe since, in these generative models, the transformer (or more generally, the denoiser) is the most computationally heavy component.

Compiling a model ahead-of-time with PyTorch involves multiple steps:.

In a recent development, recall that we’re going to compile the model ahead of time. Therefore, we need to derive example inputs for the model. Note that these are the same kinds of inputs we expect to see during the actual runs. To capture those inputs, we will leverage the spaces.aoti_capture helper from the spaces package:.

When used as a context manager, aoti_capture intercepts the call to any callable (pipe.transformer in our case), prevents it from executing, captures the input arguments that would have been passed to it, and stores their values in call.args and call.kwargs.

Now that we have example args and kwargs for our transformer component, we can export it to a PyTorch ExportedProgram by using torch.export.export utility:.

An exported PyTorch program is a computation graph that represents the tensor computations along with the original model parameter values.

Once the model is exported, compiling it is pretty straightforward.

In our case, we’ll leverage a helper function part of the spaces package: spaces.aoti_compile. This compiled_transformer is now an AoT-compiled binary ready to be used for inference.

Now we need to bind our compiled transformer to our original pipeline, i.e., the pipeline.

Unfortunately, this approach does not work because it deletes vital attributes like dtype, config, etc. Only patching the forward method does not work well either because we are then keeping original model parameters in memory, often leading to OOM errors at runtime.

If you want to learn more about AoT compilation, you can read PyTorch's AOTInductor tutorial.

Now that we have demonstrated the speedups one can realize under the constraints of operating with ZeroGPUs, we will discuss a few gotchas that came up while working with this setup.

AoT can be combined with quantization to deliver even greater speedups. For image and video generation, the FP8 post-training dynamic quantization schemes deliver good speed-quality trade-offs. However, FP8 requires a CUDA compute capability of at least 9.0 to work. Thankfully, for ZeroGPUs, since they’re based on H200s, we can already take advantage of the FP8 quantization schemes.

According to recent reports, images and videos can come in different shapes and sizes. Hence, it’s important to also account for shape dynamism when performing AoT compilation. Dynamic shapes is sometimes not enough when dynamism is too key.

This is, for instance, the case with the Wan family of video generation models if you want your compiled model to generate different resolutions. One thing can be done in this case: compile one model per resolution while keeping the model parameters shared and dispatching the right one at runtime.

Here is a minimal example of this approach: zerogpu-aoti-multi.py. You can also see a fully working implementation of this paradigm in the Wan 2.2 Space.

It has been revealed that since the ZeroGPU hardware and CUDA drivers are perfectly compatible with Flash-Attention 3 (FA3), we can use it in our ZeroGPU Spaces to speed things up even further. FA3 works with ahead-of-time compilation. So, this is ideal for our case.

According to recent reports, compiling and building FA3 from source can take several minutes, and this process is hardware-dependent. As users, we wouldn’t want to lose precious ZeroGPU compute hours. This is where Hugging Face kernels library comes to the rescue. It provides access to pre-built kernels that are compatible for a given hardware. For example, when we try to run:.

Industry observers note that it tries to load a kernel from the kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3 repository, which is compatible with the current setup. Otherwise, it will error out due to incompatibility issues. Luckily for us, this works seamlessly on the ZeroGPU Spaces. This means we can leverage the power of FA3 on ZeroGPU, using the kernels library.

Here is a fully working example of an FA3 attention processor for the Qwen-Image model.

So far, we have been compiling the full model. Depending on the model, full model compilation can lead to significantly long cold start times. Long cold start times make the development experience unpleasant.

We can also choose to compile regions within a model, significantly reducing the cold start times, while retaining almost all the benefits of full model compilation. Regional compilation becomes promising when a model has repeated blocks of computation. A standard language model, for example, has a number of identically structured Transformer blocks.

In our example, we can compile the repeated blocks of the Flux transformer ahead of time, and propagate the compiled graph to the remaining repeated blocks. The Flux Transformer has two kinds of repeated blocks: FluxTransformerBlock and FluxSingleTransformerBlock.

You can check out this Space for a complete example.

💡 For Flux.1-Dev, switching to regional compilation reduces the compilation time from 6 minutes to just 30 seconds while delivering identical speedups.

Industry observers note that once a model (or even a model block) is compiled ahead of time, we can serialize the compiled graph module as an artifact and reuse later. In the context of a ZeroGPU-powered demo on Spaces, this will significantly cut down the demo startup time by skipping the compilation time.

To keep the storage light, we can just save the compiled model graph without including any model parameters inside the artifact.

Check out this collection that indicates a full workflow of obtaining compiled model graph, pushing it to the Hub, and then using it to build a demo.

ZeroGPU within Hugging Face Spaces is a powerful feature that enables AI builders by providing access to powerful compute. In this post, we showed how people can benefit from PyTorch’s ahead-of-time compilation techniques to speed up their applications that leverage ZeroGPU.

Sources indicate that we demonstrate speedups with Flux.1-Dev, but these techniques are not limited to just this model. Therefore, we encourage you to give these techniques a try and provide us with feedback in this community discussion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a substantial neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”.
  • In a recent development, google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet.
  • That might finally be changing, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a substantial neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”.

In a recent development, google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

The newly introduced look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

Sources indicate that the most crucial thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent revision directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year-over-year in Q3 2026

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce.
  • Recent findings suggest that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments.
  • Price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce. Shipments also increased 13% sequentially, reflecting strong demand for OLED displays and improving panel availability. While the market's rapid growth is impressive regardless, there are good reasons why OLED monitors are becoming increasingly popular: they're getting cheaper, better, and considerably easier to justify.

Recent findings suggest that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments. MSI climbed into second place for the first time, capturing 14.5% of the market, while Samsung slipped to third with 11.3%. Both Taiwanese vendors have been particularly aggressive in the gaming monitor market, where increasingly competitive pricing has helped make OLED technology accessible to more buyers, while ubiquitous advertising with tech-conscious gamers has made them highly visible. According to Omdia, mainstream 27-inch QHD 240Hz OLED gaming monitors have seen price cuts exceeding 40% in 2026.

Price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though. Earlier generations of OLED monitors had some fairly significant compromises, particularly their relatively limited brightness and unconventional subpixel arrangements that could cause colored fringing around text. Newer tandem OLED panels offer improved brightness and color reproduction, while RGB-stripe OLED layouts bring much cleaner text rendering. These improvements are making OLEDs considerably more attractive as everyday desktop monitors, rather than merely excellent gaming displays with major caveats.

In a recent development, there's also an interesting macroeconomic angle to OLED's growth. The AI industry's insatiable appetite for memory and storage has made upgrading a gaming PC considerably more expensive. DRAM component prices have increased severalfold, while NAND flash and hard drive availability have also been squeezed by demand from AI data centers—though there are early signs of some relief, at least on the flash memory front. Graphics cards, especially (but not exclusively) at the high end, are increasingly difficult to find at anything resembling reasonable prices.

Monitors, meanwhile, aren't directly subject to the same supply pressures affecting DRAM, NAND, and discrete GPUs. That makes upgrading a display an appealing alternative for gamers who aren't particularly interested in spending a small fortune on an entirely latest PC. An OLED monitor can substantially improve the gaming experience without requiring a new graphics card, memory kit, or storage drive. The contrast, response times, and color gamut of OLEDs far outstrip even the best LCDs, and that's to say nothing of their superior HDR reproduction thanks to the inherent self-emissive nature of OLED panels.

With OLED prices falling and the technology's longstanding limitations becoming less noticeable, a fresh monitor is becoming one of the more compelling upgrades available to PC gamers. Indeed, several of our picks for the best gaming monitors, including the best overall, best 4K, and best ultrawide, are based on OLED technology. Though concerns about burn-in and limited lifespan remain, there's no question that OLED is the best display technology we have right now.

According to recent reports, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Industry observers note that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and prepares auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

According to recent reports, medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company notes you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Sources indicate that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

According to recent reports, own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.
