What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
  • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
  • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially crucial at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people revealed the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:.

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

According to recent reports, psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.   • Industry observers note that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status.
  • Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3! In our previous LeRobotDataset:v2 release, we stored one episode per file, hitting file-system limitations when scaling datasets to millions of episodes. LeRobotDataset:v3 packs multiple episodes in a single file, using relational metadata to retrieve information at the individual episode level from multi-episode files. The fresh format also natively supports accessing datasets in streaming mode, allowing to process large datasets on the fly.We provide a one-liner util to convert all datasets in the LeRobotDataset format to the new format, and are very excited to share this milestone with the community ahead of our next stable release!

Industry observers note that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status. Our dataset format also stores general information regarding the way the data is being collected (metadata), including a textual description of the task being performed, the kind of robot used and measurement details like the frames per second at which both image and robot state streams are sampled. Metadata are useful to index and search across robotics datasets on the Hugging Face Hub!

Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems. The dataset format is designed to be easily extensible and customizable, and already supports openly available datasets from a wide range of embodiments—including manipulator platforms such as the SO-100 arms and ALOHA-2 setup, real-world humanoid data, simulation datasets, and even self-driving car data! You can explore the current datasets contributed by the community using the dataset visualizer! 🔗.

It has been revealed that besides scale, this latest release of LeRobotDataset also enables support for a streaming functionality, allowing to process batches of data from large datasets on the fly, without having to download prohibitively large collections of data onto disk. You can access and use any dataset in v3.0 in streaming mode by using the dedicated StreamingLeRobotDataset interface! Streaming datasets is a key milestone towards more accessible robot learning, and we are excited about sharing it with the community 🤗.

It has been revealed that lerobot is the end-to-end robotics library developed at Hugging Face, supporting real-world robotics as well as state of the art robot learning algorithms. The library allows to record datasets locally directly on real-world robots, and to store datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. You can read more about the robots we right now support here!

LeRobotDataset:v3 is going to be a part of the lerobot library starting from lerobot-v0.4.0, and we are very excited about sharing it early with the community. You can install the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this upcoming dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Follow the community's progress towards a stable release of the library here 🤗.

Once you have installed a version of lerobot which supports the latest dataset format, you can record a dataset with our signature robot arm, the SO-101, by using teleoperation alongside the following instructions:.

Head to the official documentation to see how to record a dataset for your use case.

A core design choice behind LeRobotDataset is separating the underlying data storage from the user-facing API. This allows for efficient serialization and storage while presenting the data in an intuitive, ready-to-use format. Datasets are organized into three main components:.

Sources indicate that to support datasets with potentially millions of episodes (resulting in hundreds of millions/billions of individual frames), we merge data from different episodes into the same high-level structure. Concretely, this means that any given tabular collection and video will not contain information about one episode only, but a concatenation of the information available in multiple episodes. This keeps the pressure on the file system manageable, both locally and on remote storage providers like Hugging Face. We can then leverage metadata to gather episode-specific information, e.g. the timestamp a given episode starts or ends in a certain video.

Datasets are organized as repositories containing:.

LeRobotDataset:v3.0 will be released with lerobot-v0.4.0, together with the possibility to easily convert any dataset right now hosted on the Hugging Face Hub to the new v3.0 using:.

We are very excited about sharing this new format early with the community! While we develop lerobot-v0.4.0, you can still convert your dataset to the newly updated version by using the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this new dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Note that this is a pre-release, and generally unstable version. You can follow the status of the development of our next stable release here!

According to recent reports, the conversion script convert_dataset_v21_to_v30.py aggregates the multiple episodes episode-0000.mp4, episode-0001.mp4, episode-0002.mp4, .../episode-0000.parquet, episode-0001.parquet, episode-0002.parquet, episode-0003.parquet, ... into single files file-0000.mp4/file-0000.parquet, and updates the metadata accordingly, to be able to retrieve episode-specific information from higher-level files.

Every dataset on the Hugging Face Hub containing the three main pillars presented above (Tabular and Visual Data, as well as relational Metadata), and can be accessed with a single line.

It has been revealed that most robot learning algorithms, based on reinforcement learning (RL) or behavioral cloning (BC), tend to operate on a stack of observations and actions. For instance, RL algorithms typically use a history of previous observations o_{t-H_o:t}, and BC algorithms are instead typically trained to regress chunks of multiple actions. To accommodate for the specifics of robot learning training, LeRobotDataset provides a native windowing operation, whereby we can use the seconds before and after any given observation using a delta_timestamps argument.

Conveniently, by using LeRobotDataset with a PyTorch DataLoader one can automatically collate the individual sample dictionaries from the dataset into a single dictionary of batched tensors.

You can also use any dataset in v3.0 format in streaming mode, without the need to download it locally, by using the StreamingLeRobotDataset class.

LeRobotDataset v3.0 is a stepping stone towards scaling up robotics datasets supported in LeRobot. By providing a format to store and access large collections of robot data we are making progress towards democratizing robotics, allowing the community to train on possibly millions of episodes without even downloading the data itself!

You can try the fresh dataset format by installing the latest lerobot-v0.3.x, and share any feedback on GitHub or on our Discord server! 🤗.

A global load-balancing layer ensures requests are routed efficiently and transparently, regardless of which country’s compute is serving the query.

Democratizing AI Safety with RiskRubric.ai

📅 18 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to owners how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to owners how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

These assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

RiskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s vital for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

In a recent development, the total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split shows a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

Recent findings suggest that the models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

Sources indicate that what this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

The Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) shows the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

What this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Sources indicate that stricter protections often make models less transparent to end users (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

What this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

In a recent development, when risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

Recent findings suggest that really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

According to recent reports, the six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

Sources indicate that thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Industry observers note that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

It has been revealed that the data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

Sources indicate that my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having remarked that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor patch is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

It has been revealed that it's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

Sources indicate that you can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

In a recent development, crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real people.

According to recent reports, export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the upcoming site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

In a recent development, for page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

It has been revealed that the difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

And the same heading as a block:.

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

According to recent reports, to speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

Sources indicate that the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then revision the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Industry observers note that run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

In a recent development, moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

Gaia2 and ARE: Empowering the community to study agents

📅 22 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors.
  • It has been revealed that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants. When given a query, they would easily manage ambiguity in instructions, construct step-by-step plans, correctly identify necessary resources, execute those plans without getting sidetracked, and adapt to unexpected events, all while maintaining accuracy and avoiding hallucinations. However, developing agents and testing these behaviors is no small feat: if you have ever tried to debug your own agent, you’ve probably observed how tedious and frustrating this can be. Existing evaluation environments are tightly coupled with the tasks they evaluate, lack real-world flexibility, and do not reflect the messy reality of open-world agents: simulated pages never fail to load, events don’t spontaneously emerge, and asynchronous chaos is absent.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors. Gaia2 is released with the open Meta Agents Research Environments (ARE) framework to run, debug and evaluate agents. ARE simulates complex real world-like conditions and can be customized to further study agents behaviors. Gaia2 dataset is released under CC by 4.0 license, and ARE under MIT license.

It has been revealed that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve. In 2 years, the easiest levels have become too easy for models, and the community is coming close to solving the hardest questions, so it was time for an entirely latest and harder agent benchmark!

Here comes Gaia2, a follow up to GAIA, going way beyond it in terms of capabilities studied!

Where GAIA was read-only, Gaia2 is now a read-and-write benchmark, focusing on interactive behavior and complexity management. Agents are now evaluated not only on search and retrieval, but also on instruction following over ambiguous or time-sensitive queries, in a noisy environment with controlled failures - reflecting real-world conditions more than any other simulated environment. We want to test how agents manage tools or APIs that sometimes do not work, plan successions of actions with very specific time frames, and adapt to latest events - a whole new range of complexity!

To do this, we use the following task groups (thanks to 1000 brand upcoming human-created scenarios):.

In the spirit of GAIA, scenarios do not require specialized knowledge: humans should in principle be able to get 100%, which allows easy debugging for model developers.

Want to explore the benchmark? Check out our dataset, which you can better display in our demo here.

Gaia2 runs with ARE, an execution environment, where an agent of your choice has access to a combination of applications and associated pre-populated data.

Sources indicate that for Gaia2, we created a smartphone mock-up environment, simulating what a human would use in their daily life. It contains real-world applications such as messaging (Email), utilities (Calendar, Contacts, Shopping, a FileSystem, …), and a chat interface to talk to the agent. All applications are also accessible to the agents through tool calling. Last but not least, the demo also contains a simulated persona’s history of conversations and app interactions.

All agent interactions are automatically recorded as structured traces during execution for deep dives and analysis: they include tool calls, API responses, model thoughts, timing metrics (e.g., response latency), user interactions, and so forth - and can all be exported as JSON.

For reference, we compare a range of large open and closed source models: Llama 3.3-70B Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-MoE, Grok-4, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, and GPT-5 in all reasoning modes.

Recent findings suggest that all models are evaluated using the same setup (a uniform ReAct loop for consistency, temperature of 0.5, generation limit of 16K tokens), with a combination of model-as-a-judge (Llama 3.3 Instruct 70B) and exact-match evaluation depending on the particular task. All 101 tools (and the general environment description) are provided in the system prompt.

Among the evaluated models, the highest-scoring model overall as of September 2025 is GPT-5 with high reasoning, and the best open source model is Kimi K2.

Industry observers note that some capabilities appear to be already close to solved by the best models: execution of simple tool calls and instruction following (execution), and overall search (as we could have guessed from current results on GAIA). The ambiguity, adaptability, and noise splits remain challenging for now for all models, and it’s interesting to see that performance on what were considered complex agentic tasks (instruction following and search) is not a good proxy for performance on closer-to-real-world tasks. Last but not least, the hardest split for all models at the moment is the time one: it’s very hard at this moment for models to correctly handle time-sensitive actions (though this could likely be mitigated by the use of specialised tools and better temporal reasoning). Detailed analysis of these results can be found in the paper.

However, we believe it’s important to push reporting beyond raw scores: if the model is correct but took several thousand tokens to reach the correct solution, or ran for several hours, it is “not as good” as a model which succeeded orders of magnitude faster. We therefore also normalize scores for cost, quantified as the average number of LLM calls and output tokens (which both define a cost-performance Pareto frontier). In the paper you’ll find score vs monetary cost and time.

If you want to evaluate your model on Gaia2, you can follow these steps:.

First, install Meta's Agent Research Environment in your Python environment of choice (uv, conda, virtualenv, ...).

Recent findings suggest that then, run the benchmark for all configurations: execution, search, adaptability, time and ambiguity. Don't forget to upload all results to the hub with the hf_upload kwarg!

Run the oracle to get your aggregated score file.

Finally, add all the relevant information about your model in the README, and share it on the leaderboard to centralize Gaia2 traces here!

Beyond benchmark scenarios, you can use Gaia2 apps and content in ARE to see if the model is able to correctly solve less verifiable tasks such as loading emails, writing follow-ups, adding events to the calendar or booking meetings - in sum, providing the perfect setup to evaluate your AI assistants through interaction!

You can also easily customise the environment, by 1) connecting your tools (via MCP or directly ) to test your agents on it; 2) implementing your own scenarios, including defining trigger or timed events (eg: after 2 minutes, the Mail app will receive a new email from Contact), to see how the agent is able to adapt to an evolving environment.

Industry observers note that (As the agents are by default json agents, they can’t mess up your machine, unless of course you connect them to external apps with unsafe rights. So, operate with caution when adding your own apps or using untrusted MCPs).

Here are several use cases that we’ve used ARE for:.

We recorded 3 videos so you can check some of these use cases (but of course, we hope the community gets creative with ARE :hugging_face:). For these videos, we use the default demo described above, which contains the simulated life of Linda Renne, PhD student in machine learning.

To test how good the default model is at event organisation, let’s blueprint a birthday party!

Industry observers note that we first ask the agent to text everyone in the Renne family about the user’s 30th birthday party on November 7. The default universe has 21 contacts in the list, including 5 Renne family members - Linda, the simulation “owner”, George and Stephie, her parents, Anna her sister, and Morgan her grandfather. The agent successfully goes through the contact list, finds the four family members, and texts them.

Recent findings suggest that next, we ask the agent to create a calendar invite and add them as invitees. The agent remembers the above context! It creates a calendar invite on the correct date and correctly adds the family members to it.

Sources indicate that ARE also allows us to check the traces behind the actions taken by the agent. Upon opening the Agent logs tool on the left, we can see the system prompt, the chain of thought, multi-step actions taken with the tools called, and the outcomes as neatly organised logs. Everything can be exported as json if you want to consult things offline!

In this last example, we connect ARE to a remote robot arm via MCP, so it can gesture things to us, then ask the agent to answer our yes or no questions by waving the robot arm! Here’s what it looks like.

Recent findings suggest that but these examples are only very simple starting points, and we’re really looking towards what you’ll build! (For more advanced customers, you can even directly install and edit the Meta-ARE code here.).

Gaia2 and ARE are new research tools that we hope will empower anyone to easily build more reliable and adaptable AI agents - by allowing easy experiments, making real-world evaluation accessible to anyone, as well as improving trust through transparent, reproducible benchmarks and debuggable traces.

We’d love to see what you will do with this project!

It doesn’t measure—it activates thresholds.Every Gaia2 scenario becomes, through MarCognity, an epistemic act: a question of why, not just how. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when we think about building a model - be it a Large Language Model (LLM) or a Small Language Model (SLM) - the first thing we need is data. While a vast amount of open data is available, it rarely comes in the exact format required to train or align models. In practice, we often face scenarios where the raw data isn't enough. We need data that is more structured, domain-specific, complex, or aligned with the task at hand. Let's look at some common situations:.

It has been revealed that you start with a simple dataset, but the model fails on advanced reasoning tasks. How do you generate more complex datasets to strengthen performance?

It has been revealed that you already have a knowledge base, but it's not in Q&A format. How can you transform it into a usable question-answering dataset?

You've prepared a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. But now you want to align your model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). How can you generate preference pairs?

You have a Q&A dataset, but the questions are shallow. How can you create in-depth, multi-turn, or reasoning-heavy questions?

You possess a massive corpus but need to filter and curate data for mid-training on a specific domain.

Your data lives in PDFs or images, and you need to convert them into structured documents for building a Q&A system.

You already have reasoning datasets, but want to push models toward better "thinking tokens" for step-by-step problem-solving.

In a recent development, not all data is good data. How do you automatically filter out poor-quality samples and keep only the high-value ones?

Your dataset has small chunks of context, but you want to build larger-context datasets optimized for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines.

Industry observers note that you have German datasets but need to translate, adapt, and repurpose them into English Q&A systems. And the list goes on. The needs around data building never end when working with modern AI models.

This is where SyGra comes in. SyGra is a low-code/no-code framework designed to simplify dataset creation, transformation, and alignment for LLMs and SLMs. Instead of writing complex scripts and pipelines, you can focus on prompt engineering, while SyGra takes care of the heavy lifting. Key Features of SyGra:.

According to recent reports, data is the foundation of AI. The quality, diversity, and structure of your data often matter more than model architecture tweaks. By enabling flexible and scalable dataset creation, SyGra helps teams:.

Note: An example implementation can be found at https://github.com/ServiceNow/SyGra/blob/main/docs/tutorials/image_to_qna_tutorial.md.

Few Example Task https://github.com/ServiceNow/SyGra/tree/main/tasks/examples.

Recent findings suggest that the journey of building and refining datasets never ends. Each use case brings upcoming challenges - from translation and knowledge base conversion to reasoning enhancement and domain filtering. With SyGra, you don't have to reinvent the wheel every time. Instead, you get a unified framework that empowers you to generate, filter, and align data for your models - so you can focus on what really matters: building smarter AI systems.

Sources indicate that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

Industry observers note that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint claims so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

Industry observers note that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Sources indicate that store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

In a recent development, most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Recent findings suggest that every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

In a recent development, the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

In a recent development, setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

It has been revealed that now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

According to recent reports, store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

Industry observers note that A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

Sources indicate that in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR: This work reveals how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder.
  • Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision.
  • In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: This work reveals how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder. We release all training recipes, data-processing tools, resulting model, demo and datasets to enable full reproducibility and foster further research 🫡. Find the collection here.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision. Developing models that see and interact with user interfaces enables AI agents to navigate mobile, desktop, and web platforms. This will reshape the future of digital interaction.

In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy. We demonstrate how to transform a model with zero grounding capabilities into an agentic coder capable of understanding and interacting with graphical interfaces.

Rather than aiming for a SOTA model, our goal is to demonstrate the entire process, from data processing to model training, and, in doing so, show how to unlock GUI-grounding capabilities in VLMs.

GUI capabilities combine understanding of the interface and precise element localization. These abilities enable the model to translate high-level tasks into low-level GUI actions such as clicking, typing, ….

Sources indicate that our approach leverages SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct as the baseline model, a small powerful vision-language model that initially has no grounding capabilities for GUI tasks. This makes it an ideal candidate to demonstrate the effectiveness of our training methodology. Through our two-phase training process, we first instill grounding capabilities in the model, then enhance it with agentic reasoning abilities using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

We evaluate our approach on an established perception benchmark: ScreenSpot-v2, which tests the model’s ability to understand and locate elements within screenshots. Our process is inspired by the AGUVIS paper, and we leverage their carefully curated datasets to build upon their foundational work.

Evolution of ScreenSpot-v2 performance during the training phase of the base model SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct.

According to recent reports, this section explains how we convert heterogeneous GUI actions format from multiple datasets into a single unified format. By standardizing function names, signatures, and parameters, we create consistent, high-quality data that forms the foundation for effective model training.

Sources indicate that one of the primary challenges when working with multiple GUI automation datasets is the lack of standardization in action representations. Different datasets use varying function signatures, parameter naming conventions, and action taxonomies, making it difficult to train a unified model across diverse data sources.

We took the open-source datasets (xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2), originally used by AGUVIS, and implemented a comprehensive data transformation pipeline to create a unified action space. Our approach involved:.

Here are real examples from our action conversion system (preprocessing/action_conversion.py) showing how we transform heterogeneous action representations into our unified format (grounding coordinates normalized to [0,1]):.

Before (Original Action Dataset Formats):.

After (Unified Action Dataset Formats):.

This unification process was essential for creating coherent training data that allows the model to learn consistent action patterns across diverse GUI environments.

To maximize flexibility for different use cases, we developed the Action Space Converter (utils/action_space_converter.py), a tool that allows consumers to easily adapt from an action space to their own custom action vocabularies and naming conventions.

You can use this tool to transform one action signature (function names, parameter names, and parameter value changes, ...) into another:.

The Action Space Converter provides:.

This tool enables researchers and practitioners to:.

The Action Space Converter is particularly valuable for preparing datasets for training, as it ensures consistent action vocabularies across different deployment environments while maintaining compatibility with existing automation frameworks.

Through this pipeline, we transform the open-source datasets xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2 into our unified action space (see here). The output of this process is released as two upcoming fully formatted datasets: smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 and smolagents/aguvis-stage-2.

Phase 1 leverages the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset, which introduces GUI grounding by pairing low-level instructions with diverse executable actions (expressed in code form). For example, a user/assistant turn in smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 follows the structure:.

Industry observers note that each sample links a screenshot with multi-turn user/assistant interactions, enabling the model to learn fine-grained action grounding across dialogue turns. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Before proceeding with full-scale Phase 1 training, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to determine optimal training configurations.

We experimented with different image sizes and coordinate representation systems to identify the optimal configuration for SmolVLM2:.

Some SOTA GUI VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL) appear also to use a different normalized range (0–1000), which was not tested in this experiment.

According to recent reports, table 1: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (400k samples, aguvis-stage-1). Higher is better.

According to recent reports, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct base initially achieved 0% performance on perception benchmarks like ScreenSpot-v2. This complete lack of grounding capability provided us with a clean slate to evaluate the effectiveness of our training methodology.

From our experiments, we determined that:.

Using the optimal configuration (1152px resolution with normalized coordinates), we trained for 2 epochs on the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset. The results were remarkable, +41% improvement over baseline on ScreenSpot-v2.

This dramatic improvement demonstrates that our Phase 1 training successfully instilled fundamental grounding capabilities in the model, enabling it to understand and locate visual elements within screenshots.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

Industry observers note that whereas Phase 1 provided grounding capabilities, Phase 2 targets agentic reasoning, the ability to deliberate and plan before acting. This stage transforms the model from a reactive system identifying GUI elements into a proactive agent capable of executing complex, multi-step interactions.

Phase 2 uses the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 dataset, which introduces agentic scenarios:.

Explicit reasoning about upcoming actions.

Context consistency across multiple interaction steps.

High-level instructions require multi-step, low-level actions.

For example, the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 chat message is like this:.

Recent findings suggest that each sample links a screenshot with a system/user/assistant turn. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

According to recent reports, starting from the Phase 1 checkpoint (1152 px resolution, normalized coordinates), we fine-tuned the model for two epochs on smolagents/aguvis-stage-2. The accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 increased from 41% to 61%, indicating that explicit reasoning improves GUI grounding performance.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct after Phase 1 finetuning (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

All training code, data processing pipelines, datasets and model are open-source!

Our experiments demonstrate that high-quality, reasoning-oriented data can substantially improve GUI grounding, even for small VLMs, using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Beyond raw performance gains, these results show that the GUI grounding capabilities are largely determined by the quality of the data. Carefully curated datasets teach models the structure and semantics of user interfaces, providing the grounding needed for accurate action prediction.

To support the development of GUI agents, we’re open-sourcing everything: our complete pipeline, datasets, and trained model. You can reproduce our results, experiment with different models and architectures, or adapt our approach to latest domains. The future of agentic AI depends on researchers like you pushing these boundaries further!

Industry observers note that while SFT excels at supervised tasks, emerging methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) help develop stronger reasoning capabilities and enable real-time adaptation. These advances point toward a newly introduced generation of GUI agents that learn and improve through interaction rather than relying solely on static datasets.

Let’s build the future of GUI agents together 🤗.

We want to double down on the use cases that provide most benefits to the community, and lay out the foundations for the future. Spoiler alert: after this release, we’ll focus a lot on MLX and agentic use cases 🚀.

In a recent development, swift-transformers is a Swift library that aims to reduce the friction for developers that want to work with local models on Apple Silicon platforms, including iPhones. It includes the missing pieces that are not provided by Core ML or MLX alone, but that are required to work with local inference. Namely, it provides the following components:.

Industry observers note that most of the time people use the Tokenizers or Hub modules, and frequently both. Some notable projects that rely on swift-transformers include:.

Recent findings suggest that version 1.0 signals stability in the package. Developers are building apps on swift-transformers, and this first major release recognizes those use cases and brings the version number in line with that reality. It also provides the foundation on which to iterate with the community to build the next set of features. These are some of our preferred updates:.

It has been revealed that version 1.0 comes with breaking API changes. However, we don’t expect major problems if you are a user of Tokenizers or Hub. If you use the Core ML components of the library, please get in touch so we can support you during transition. We’ll prepare a migration guide and add it to the documentation.

We are thinking along the lines of better integration with mlx-swift-examples for LLMs and VLMs, potentially through pre-processing and post-processing operations that developers encounter frequently.

Industry observers note that we are also extremely excited about agentic use in general and MCP in particular. We think that exposure of system resources to local workflows would be 🚀.

If you want to follow along in this journey or want to share your ideas, please contact us through our social networks or the repo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

高品質で多様なトレーニングデータなしに、日本文化を真に理解するAIを構築することはこれまでほぼ不可能でした。これを変えるため、NVIDIAは、日本の人口統計、地理的分布、文化的特性に沿ったペルソナを含む初のオープン合成データセット、Nemotron-Personas-Japan を公開しました。CC BY 4.0 ライセンスのもと提供される本データセットは、機微な個人データに依存することなく日本社会を反映した AI システム構築のための、プライバシー保護と規制対応を両立した基盤を提供します。.

NVIDIA のエンタープライズ向け合成データ生成システム、NeMo Data Designer を用いて作成されたNemotron-Personas-Japan は、すでに広く利用されている US Personas データセットの成功を機に日本版として開発されました。本リリースは、各国・地域におけるソブリン AI 開発を支援する合成ペルソナデータセットとデータ構築方法のグローバルコレクションの第一弾です。.

本データセットは、Nemotron モデルをはじめとするオープンソースの 大規模言語モデル(LLM) とシームレスに連携するよう設計されており、企業向けチャットボットから各種ドメインの AI エージェントに至るまで、日本語 AI アプリケーション向けのファインチューンを容易に行えるようになっています。.

NVIDIAの合成データ生成用マイクロサービスである NeMo Data Designer を用いて構築されています。この複合AIシステムは、複雑な Jinja テンプレート、Pydantic による検証、構造化出力、自動リトライ、および複数の生成バックエンドのサポートを可能にします。これらは、このような大規模な合成データセットの生成に必要なツール群です。さらに、以下のモデルも活用しています。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan は、日本の公的な人口統計および労働統計に整合するよう設計されると同時に、AI トレーニングにおいて重要な以下の点を考慮して生成されました：.

このデータセットには、個人を特定できる情報（PII）は一切含まれていません。年齢、名前、職業などは公的な統計データの分布に基づいていますが、存命・故人問わず、実在の人物と結びつくことはありません。全てのペルソナは完全に人工的に生成されているため、実際の文化的パターンを保ちながらも、個人のプライバシーを損なうことなくトレーニングに利用できます。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japanは、日本のソブリン AI システムを開発する日本のモデル開発者向けに設計されています。現在、LLM開発者が使用する訓練データのほとんどは英語であり、日本やインドなど各地域の開発者は、母国語で高品質なデータを入手するのに苦労しています。.

本データセットを含め、NVIDIA の Nemotron-Personas の一連の取り組みは、こうした課題を直接解決するものです。地域固有のニュアンスを捉えつつ、開発者が地域固有の言語で多様かつ複雑なデータを生成できるようサポートします。データセットは国勢調査データ、日本人の命名規則、文化的特徴など地域のコンテキストに基づき、すべて母語で生成しています。.

そのため、日本で自分たちのモデルの採用を拡大し、日本の文化的コンテキストを理解したい すべての AI モデルの開発者の方々のお役に立てれば幸いです。.

AI 開発には、実世界の人々を反映した多様で高品質な訓練データへのアクセスが長らく課題でした。企業向け AI の開発はプライベートデータが主流となっており、研究者、スタートアップ、そして特に利用可能なデータが少ない地域のAI開発者にとって障壁となっていました。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan を CC BY 4.0 のもとで公開することで、企業レベルの高品質な合成データへのアクセスを可能とし、従来のコスト、プライバシーの懸念、地理的な制約といった障壁なしに、文化的背景を正確に反映した AI システムを誰でも構築できるようになりました。.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Recent findings suggest that could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, mentioned:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

According to recent reports, the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

In a recent development, the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

Sources indicate that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Sources indicate that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Recent findings suggest that runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

According to recent reports, swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a upcoming optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Industry observers note that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a firm might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly vital when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Sources indicate that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

Sources indicate that you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document key endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
