📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that people are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

First, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

It has been revealed that however, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

According to recent reports, earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very swiftly.

To address this matter, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Sources indicate that anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

According to recent reports, the official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

In a recent development, roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

Recent findings suggest that the unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

Sources indicate that this approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

This will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

Here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

So, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires consumers to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

Recent findings suggest that then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

The engine is currently very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

It's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what's going on in the space!

This is very cool! A mini-engine with API designed for LLMs may be able to supercharge game development.

For anyone interested in exploring what's already being built, we've been collecting the best AI-Assisted and vibe-coded games on VibeTopList. Feel free to check for yourself https://vibetoplist.com/.

I've been working on something along similar lines, called Rosh.

It has been revealed that it covers some of the things you list as missing. Rooms are multiplayer and live: people and AI agents can be in the same room changing it together. The same room works in real time in your browser (three.js), a terminal, Unity and Unreal Engine. It also reads the room back to the AI as text, with notes on what looks wrong, so agents can fix their own object placement etc.

Latest Update: Accelerating Qwen3-8B Agent on Intel® Core™ Ultra with Depth-Pruned Draft Models

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

Sources indicate that qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

Speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

Before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

In a recent development, the speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Our recent work shows that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

The resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

To showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

Introducing RTEB: A Latest Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • It has been revealed that this is where things get tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

Recent findings suggest that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

It has been revealed that this is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on new, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following issues:.

Sources indicate that the Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

Because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to new problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

Misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these challenges are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

Sources indicate that today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a fresh, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

Sources indicate that this hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

Recent findings suggest that A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We plan to continually upgrade both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an issue on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

Industry observers note that RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we blueprint to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest new datasets, find issues in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an matter in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our plans for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

The RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the upcoming Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

[1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Industry observers note that is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (right now denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

It has been revealed that the discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets shows why a single retrieval average can hide important differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Sources indicate that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real people can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

It has been revealed that the Free blueprint is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app owners, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Recent findings suggest that lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

In a recent development, base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

In a recent development, bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

According to recent reports, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

In a recent development, core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Industry observers note that glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

It has been revealed that glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web aims run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Sources indicate that retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

Sources indicate that v0's Free proposal gives upcoming people $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Industry observers note that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter strategy is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Industry observers note that collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

It has been revealed that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

In a recent development, agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human consumers.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

Recent findings suggest that whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

It has been revealed that in this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

Industry observers note that to follow along, clone the repo. You'll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:.

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:.

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

Sources indicate that dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

Recent findings suggest that when kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

Once we've done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:.

The model doesn't require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

Recent findings suggest that using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:.

cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It's derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call, commit here.

Recent findings suggest that and there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:.

which will launch the XCode inspector for the model. After clicking + Performance Report and launching a report on all compute devices, you should see something like the following:.

Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight.
  • According to recent reports, permissions alone can't catch this.
  • Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

According to recent reports, permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

Sources indicate that today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

If the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a proposal, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

BigCodeArena: Judging code generations end to end with code executions

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult.
  • Sources indicate that inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces.
  • The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult. While humans can easily spot whether a piece of code "looks right," determining if it actually works correctly, handles edge cases properly, and produces the intended result requires running and testing it. This is why today, we're thrilled to announce BigCodeArena -- the first human-in-the-loop platform for evaluating code generation models through execution.

Sources indicate that inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces. Just submit a coding task, watch two different models generate solutions, execute both programs, and vote on which model produced better results. The outcomes are organized into a leaderboard that displays the community's highest-rated models.

The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods. Traditional benchmarks like HumanEval test code against predefined test cases, but these represent only a tiny fraction of real-world programming tasks. Human evaluation platforms exist for general chatbots, but they fall short for code: reading raw source code and mentally simulating its execution is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially for longer programs or complex UI applications.

Recent findings suggest that you ask two AI models to build a responsive photo gallery website. Both generate code that looks syntactically correct. But which one is actually better? Without running the code, it's nearly impossible to tell. One might produce a beautiful, functional grid layout, while the other might have subtle bugs or poor styling that only become apparent when rendered in a browser.

This observation led us to a key insight: execution feedback is essential for humans to judge code quality reliably. That's exactly what BigCodeArena provides.

BigCodeArena extends the Chatbot Arena framework with powerful features specifically designed for code evaluation:.

Every code snippet generated by models is automatically executed in isolated sandbox environments. Whether it's a Python script, a React web app, a PyGame game, or a C++ algorithm, you can see the actual output, not just the source code.

We at the moment support 10 languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, C, C++, Java, Go, Rust, and Markdown) and 8 execution environments:.

Unlike static code comparison, you can actually interact with the generated applications:.

Real programming isn't one-and-done. BigCodeArena supports multi-turn interactions, allowing you to refine requirements, ask for features to be added, or request bug fixes -- just like working with a real coding assistant.

Since launching in February 2025, BigCodeArena has collected over 14,000 conversations from more than 500 unique owners, with 4,700+ high-quality preference votes comparing 10 frontier LLMs.

Our customers have explored remarkably diverse coding scenarios:.

Sources indicate that python dominates with over 4,000 conversations, followed by JavaScript/TypeScript (3,359), HTML (1,601), and C++ (642). Among frameworks, direct Python interpreters lead usage (6,000 sessions), with React (2,729), Core Web (1,574), Streamlit (1,254), and PyGame (1,087) also seeing heavy use.

In a recent development, most interactions are focused and efficient: 76% of conversations consist of just 2 turns (one request, one response), with a mean conversation length of 4.12 messages. However, the platform supports extended multi-turn debugging sessions when needed, with some conversations exceeding 10 turns as customers refine complex applications.

According to recent reports, from our 14K conversations, we filtered for high-quality pairwise comparisons: conversations with at least two turns and actual code execution. This yielded 4,731 voting samples, with each evaluated model receiving at least 700 votes. We aggregate these votes into Elo ratings using the Bradley-Terry model, which estimates the probability that one model beats another based on head-to-head comparisons.

To ensure robust rankings, we use 100 bootstrap resamples to construct 95% confidence intervals, so we can identify statistically significant performance differences between models.

We evaluate models under three settings to control for different factors:.

Rankings remain remarkably consistent across all three settings, revealing clear performance tiers:.

According to recent reports, top Tier: o3-mini and o1-mini consistently lead with the highest Elo ratings and tight confidence intervals. These models maintain top performance regardless of environment or language constraints, showing strong robustness across coding scenarios. Claude-3.5-Sonnet follows closely, particularly excelling when language is controlled.

In a recent development, mid Tier: GPT-4o, o1, and Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash form a competitive middle tier. GPT-4o shows some sensitivity to language matching, suggesting room for improvement in multilingual consistency.

Open Source Models: Qwen2.5 variants and Llama-3.3-70B lag behind frontier proprietary models, highlighting the performance gap that remains between leading closed and open models.

Figure: Overall win rate heatmaps (percentage of all pairwise comparisons won) of each model in the sessions across languages (left) and execution environments (right). For each category, we only keep models that appear in at least 3 conversation sessions.

Breaking down performance by programming language reveals interesting patterns:.

Analyzing win rates by execution environment reveals how models handle different runtime contexts:.

Robust Performers: o3-mini maintains consistently strong performance across React, Streamlit, Gradio, Core Web, and PyGame, demonstrating excellent environmental adaptability.

Stable but Selective: Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.0-Flash show generally stable performance but with reduced win rates in complex UI-heavy environments like Vue and Mermaid.

It has been revealed that framework-Specific Weaknesses: Qwen2.5 models, while competitive in some web frameworks (Core Web, React), struggle significantly with interactive and visualization-oriented environments like PyGame, Vue, and Mermaid. These environments often require precise handling of control flow, graphics rendering, and package dependencies.

Industry observers note that these results highlight an vital insight: aggregate Elo scores don't tell the whole story. Some models remain brittle under specific runtime constraints, and execution environment matters significantly for real-world deployment.

To advance research beyond crowdsourced evaluation, we're releasing two complementary benchmarks:.

Building on our 4,700+ preference votes, BigCodeReward tests how well LLMs can judge code quality when acting as reward models. The key finding? Execution results dramatically improve judgment accuracy.

When models can see execution outputs (screenshots of web apps, game visuals, program logs), their alignment with human preferences increases substantially:.

This reinforces our core thesis: you can't reliably judge code without running it -- and this applies to both humans and AI judges.

Inspired by Arena-Hard-Auto, AutoCodeArena provides a scalable way to evaluate new models without waiting for thousands of human votes. We carefully selected 600 representative prompts from our crowdsourced data, spanning all programming topics and frameworks.

Recent findings suggest that using automated LLM judges (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) to evaluate code execution results against a GPT-4.1 baseline, we can rapidly benchmark new models. This approach enables weekly leaderboard updates as new models are released.

Our automated benchmark evaluated 20+ cutting-edge models, including recently released systems:.

Recent findings suggest that figure: Win rates of recent LLMs on AutoCodeArena against a GPT-4.1 baseline, judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The 50% mark represents parity with GPT-4.1. Models above this line outperform the baseline, while those below underperform. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Note: Claude-3.7-Sonnet is excluded from rankings to avoid self-judgment bias, and GPT-4.1 appears only as the reference baseline.

The results show that while proprietary models maintain an edge, open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, with some approaching GPT-4.1-level performance.

BigCodeArena is open to everyone -- no account required! Visit https://huggingface.co/spaces/bigcode/arena to:.

Whether you're building a React dashboard, creating a PyGame game, solving algorithmic challenges, or generating creative visualizations, BigCodeArena lets you see which models truly deliver.

Following the BigCode Project's commitment to transparency, we're releasing:.

We envision BigCodeArena as a long-term project that evolves with the community:.

Evaluating code isn't like evaluating text -- you need to run it, test it, and interact with it. BigCodeArena makes this possible at scale, combining human judgment with real execution feedback to create the most reliable evaluation platform for code generation models.

Join us in building the future of code generation evaluation. Write a prompt, compare the models, and vote for your favorite. Your feedback helps the entire community understand which models truly deliver on the promise of AI-assisted programming.

Sources indicate that we'd love to hear your feedback! Connect with us on GitHub, join discussions in the Hugging Face Space community tab, or reach out to the BigCode Project at contact@bigcode-project.org.

We thank Leandro von Werra for his valuable suggestions and feedback on the blog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

According to recent reports, • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

According to recent reports, cudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it claims it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your proposal. It indicates to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

In a recent development, GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

In a recent development, strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and indicates other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The manufacturer’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and strategy prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

According to recent reports, copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it indicates it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid initiative prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Sources indicate that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Sources indicate that strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, states very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Recent findings suggest that strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

It has been revealed that limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

In a recent development, sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

According to recent reports, strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page claims false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Sources indicate that • False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

According to recent reports, • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

In a recent development, • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

Recent findings suggest that • Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

Sources indicate that • Moving targets. Upcoming models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

According to recent reports, • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

Industry observers note that • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and enhancement as newly introduced models appear.

Industry observers note that • Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

It has been revealed that • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

In a recent development, because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

Recent findings suggest that group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

It has been revealed that • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

It has been revealed that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

Industry observers note that • Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

Recent findings suggest that • Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

Industry observers note that they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Recent findings suggest that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

In a recent development, sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

Sources indicate that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

It has been revealed that AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While running AI models on your own device can be difficult as these models are often computationally demanding, it also offers significant benefits: including improved privacy since your data stays on your machine, and enhanced speed and reliability because you're not dependent on an internet connection or external servers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with the growing capability of large language models (LLMs), a new class of models has emerged: Vision Language Models (VLMs). These models can analyze images and videos to describe scenes, create captions, and answer questions about visual content.

While running AI models on your own device can be difficult as these models are often computationally demanding, it also offers significant benefits: including improved privacy since your data stays on your machine, and enhanced speed and reliability because you're not dependent on an internet connection or external servers. This is where tools like Optimum Intel and OpenVINO come in, along with a small, efficient model like SmolVLM. In this blog post, we'll walk you through three easy steps to get a VLM running locally, with no expensive hardware or GPUs required (though you can run all the code samples from this blog post on Intel GPUs).

Small models like SmolVLM are built for low-resource consumption, but they can be further optimized. In this blog post we will see how to optimize your model, to lower memory usage and speedup inference, making it more efficient for deployment on devices with limited resources.

To follow this tutorial, you need to install optimum and openvino, which you can do with:.

First, you will need to convert your model to the OpenVINO IR. There are multiple options to do it:.

Industry observers note that now it’s time to optimize your model. Quantization reduces the precision of the model weights and/or activations, leading to smaller, faster models. Essentially, it's a way to map values from a high-precision data type, such as 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32), to a lower-precision format, typically 8-bit integers (INT8). While this process offers several key benefits, it can also impact in a potential loss of accuracy.

Optimum supports two main post-training quantization methods:.

Weight-only quantization means that only the weights are quantized but activations remain in their original precisions. As a result, the model becomes smaller and more memory-efficient, improving loading times. But since activations are not quantized, inference speed gains are limited. Weight-only quantization is a simple first step since it usually doesn’t result in significant accuracy degradation.

Since OpenVINO 2024.3, if the model's weight have been quantized, the corresponding activations will also be quantized at runtime, leading to additional speedup depending on the device.

In order to run it, you will need to create a quantization configuration OVWeightQuantizationConfig as follows:.

With Static Quantization, both weights and activations are quantized before inference. To achieve the best estimate for the activation quantization parameters, we perform a calibration step. During this step, a small representative dataset is fed through the model. In our case, we will use 50 samples of the contextual dataset and will apply static quantization on the vision encoder while weight-only quantization will be applied on the rest of the model. Experiments show that applying static quantization on the vision encoder provides a noticeable performance improvement without significant accuracy degradation. Since the vision encoder is called only once per generation, the overall performance gain from applying static quantization on this component is lower than the gain achieved by optimizing more frequently used components like the language model. Nevertheless, this approach can be beneficial in certain scenarios. For example, when short answers are needed, especially with multiple images as input.

Quantizing activations adds small errors that can build up and affect accuracy, so careful testing afterward is key. More information and examples can be found in our documentation.

You can now run inference with your quantized model:.

If you have a recent Intel laptop, Intel AI PC, or Intel discrete GPU, you can load the model on GPU by adding device="gpu" when loading your model:.

We also created a space so you can play with the original model and its quantized variants obtained by respectively applying weight-only quantization and mixed quantization. This demo runs on 4th Generation Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) processors.

To reproduce our results, check out our notebook.

We ran a benchmark to compare the performance of the PyTorch, OpenVINO, and OpenVINO 8-bit WOQ versions of the original model. The goal was to evaluate the impact of weight-only quantization on latency and throughput on Intel CPU hardware. For this test, we used a single image as input.

We measured the following metrics to evaluate the model's performance:.

Here are the results on Intel CPU:.

This benchmark demonstrates how small, optimized multimodal models, like SmolVLM2-256M, perform on Intel CPUs across different configurations. According to the tests, the PyTorch version reveals high latency, with a time to first token (TTFT) of over 5s with a decoding throughput of 0.7 tokens/s. Simply converting the model with Optimum and running it on OpenVINO drastically reduces the time to first token (TTFT) to 0.42s (x12 speedup) and raises throughput to 47 tokens/s (x65). Applying 8-bit weight-only quantization further reduces TTFT (x1.7) and increases throughput (x1.4), while also reducing model size and improving efficiency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to demonstrate the real-world value of upgrading to Google’s latest C4 Virtual Machine (VM) running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors (codenamed Granite Rapids (GNR)). We specifically wanted to benchmark improvements in the text generation performance of OpenAI GPT OSS Large Language Model(LLM).

The results are in, and they are impressive, demonstrating a 1.7x improvement in Total Cost of Ownership(TCO) over the previous-generation Google C3 VM instances. The Google Cloud C4 VM instance further resulted in:.

Industry observers note that GPT OSS is a common name for an open-source Mixture of Experts (MoE) model released by OpenAI. An MoE model is a deep neural network architecture that uses specialized “expert” sub-networks and a “gating network” to decide which experts to use for a given input. MoE models allow you to scale your model capacity efficiently without linearly scaling compute costs. They also allow for specialization, where different “experts” learn different skills, allowing them to adapt to diverse data distributions.

Even with very large parameters, only a small subset of experts is activated per token, making CPU inference viable.

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to merge an expert execution optimization (PR #40304) to eliminate redundant computation where every expert processed all tokens to transformers. This optimization directed each expert to run only on the tokens it is routed to, removing FLOPs waste and improving utilization.

We benchmarked GPT OSS under a controlled, repeatable generation workload to isolate architectural differences (GCP C4 VMs on Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) vs GCP C3 VMs on 4th Gen Intel Xeon Processors (SPR)) and MoE execution efficiency. The focus is steady‑state decoding (per‑token latency) and end‑to‑end normalized throughput with increasing batch size while keeping sequence lengths fixed. All runs use static KV cache and SDPA attention for determinism.

Google Cloud C4 VMs powered by Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) provide both impressive performance gains and better cost efficiency for large MoE inference over previous generation Google Cloud C3 VM (powered by 4th Gen Intel Xeon processors). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests indicated low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).
