  • On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.
  • Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No financial details, but plenty of other clues.

Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

“We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”.

Mastercard previously remarked that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

It has been revealed that according to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said.

It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

It has been revealed that plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26.

Industry observers note that “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he remarked. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”.

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security firm Sentra.

In that attack, which the threat hunters mentioned began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”.

Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®.

Going from a model page to deploying on Vertex Model Garden or GKE should only take a couple steps. Taking a private model securely hosted in an Enterprise organization on Hugging Face should be as easy as working with public models.

TPUs, Google custom AI accelerator chips now in their seventh generation, have been steadily improving in performance and software stack maturity. We want to make sure Hugging Face consumers can fully benefit from the current and the next generations of TPUs when they build AI with open models. We are excited to make TPUs as easy to use as GPUs for Hugging Face models, thanks to native support in our libraries.

We are excited to make this future happen with Google Cloud. Our deep collaboration will accelerate this vision, whether you are using Vertex AI Model Garden, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run or Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual patch clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay.
  • On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.
  • For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual patch clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay.

On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.

For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. People of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to enhancement their PHP instances.

The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep.

In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings.

Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults.

Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.”.

In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline.

Sources indicate that code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit.

For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote.

According to recent reports, collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry.

The newly introduced release brings some other security-minded changes as well.

It has been revealed that the PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight.

Recent findings suggest that continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs.

Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of newly introduced goodies.

PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability.

The latest edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range.

For administrators, this PHP revision round may be a bit of a shambles.

As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves.

“In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the fresh default,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®.

Itâs July 2026, and part of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is now in effect; the remainder is imminent. The new EU regulations aim to significantly improve the cybersecurity of connected products placed on the European market. If your organization develops digital products such as IoT devices or EV chargers, youâre affected.

According to recent reports, earlier this month Marc and I had the opportunity to deliver a talk at ONE Conference in The Hague, The Netherlands, on a topic thatâs near to our hearts: memory safety. Below we share some context, as well as our slides.

Weâve been raising awareness of the importance of using memory-safe technology to build systems that are truly secure-by-design. We do this alongside our core business, which is to help companies to use Rust successfully. With the CRA standardization process well on its way, now is the perfect time to upgrade you on what weâve been doing and why.

#57726. METR Finds AI Time Horizons Doubling as Research Judgment Lags

METR Finds AI Time Horizons Doubling as Research Judgment Lags

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • METR reported on November 20, 2026, that public frontier models’ 50% time horizons—the human-estimated task duration at which a model is predicted to succeed half the time, not how long the model itself works—are doubling roughly every 110 days across its combined TH1.1 and TH2 evaluations.
  • It has been revealed that the patch covers public models through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and examines capabilities relevant to automating AI research and development (R&D).
  • In a recent development, METR estimates a 95% confidence interval of 2.08 to 4.94 months for the combined doubling time, close to the previous 105-day trend for TH1.1 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

METR reported on November 20, 2026, that public frontier models’ 50% time horizons—the human-estimated task duration at which a model is predicted to succeed half the time, not how long the model itself works—are doubling roughly every 110 days across its combined TH1.1 and TH2 evaluations. The expanded testing shows strong gains on verifiable work but weaker judgment on open-ended research and evaluation design.

It has been revealed that the patch covers public models through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and examines capabilities relevant to automating AI research and development (R&D). METR typically evaluated 15 models on TH1.1 and TH2. The new TH2 suite contains 36 tasks in 12 families: eight verifiable families with well-defined, automatically scored objectives across optimization, machine learning, puzzles and games, and four families covering conceptual reasoning, judgment and open-ended research without a cheap check for success.

In a recent development, METR estimates a 95% confidence interval of 2.08 to 4.94 months for the combined doubling time, close to the previous 105-day trend for TH1.1 alone. Because TH2 is harder at a fixed human task duration, a model’s 50% time horizon on the combined suite is lower than on TH1.1 alone.

It has been revealed that on TH2’s verifiable subset, the estimated doubling time falls to 1.65 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.79 to 3.99 months. METR cautions that this noisy result could reflect task composition, a restricted date range or selection during task development rather than broad acceleration. Less diverse task sets may also produce faster doubling because longer tasks require more of the same skills.

Human calibration is less direct than in METR’s earlier work. Researchers defined score-and-time thresholds for 34 of the upcoming tasks, using successful human baselines for three and researcher estimates for 31; direct baselines informed only 9% of human-duration estimates. The specialists were paid $200 to $350 per hour and could use Sonnet 5 for implementation. METR reports similar doubling-time results after adding noise to task-time estimates and substituting model-estimated human completion times, though it remains uncertain how comparable the baseliners were to frontier-lab researchers.

On verifiable TH2 tasks, METR estimates current public frontier models’ time horizons at up to 27 hours. On each of the three formally baselined tasks, the best model outperformed every recruited human baseliner.

Larger pools of human data show that top experts can still finish ahead. Across 15 Al Zimmermann optimization contests, METR reports that the strongest models placed at the 96th to 98th percentile of human participants in the median contest, while roughly four humans beat them. Agents had 48 hours on a 28-core machine; human participants had about three months and their own hardware, so the rankings depend on those different conditions.

On Budget NanoGPT, METR reports a best autonomous-agent speedup of 15.7% in 48 hours, compared with a 41% speedup over the previous record by a recent AI-assisted human contributor who estimated spending about 60 hours. The comparison is rough because human records build sequentially on earlier work, but it shows autonomous agents trailing the strongest human result while exceeding many other competent speedrunners.

The hard-to-verify tasks reveal a different limitation. In Making METR Tasks, agents had to design an informative fresh task for METR’s own suite. METR classified some recent outputs as borderline useful, but none warranted inclusion in the suite used in the report. Models generally created automatically scored optimization tasks even when instructed to emphasize decisions with poor short-term feedback. Despite internet access, they did not independently investigate what METR would find useful, produce novel threat modeling, or base tasks on particularly insightful hypotheses about model capabilities. Those ratings rest on METR’s own research and threat-modeling judgments.

A related experiment examined whether models could score those outputs reliably. METR found that model judges agreed more closely with human ratings when assessing weaker models’ outputs, but awarded inappropriately high scores to work from similarly strong or stronger models. Opus 5.5, the judge with the highest human agreement, scored GPT-6 Astra’s tasks about 0.2 points higher than the human scorer on a one-point scale.

In a recent development, these results do not establish a universal judgment deficit. METR states models may be underelicited on judgment tasks because they underused token limits and available affordances, and notes that frontier models displayed good judgment of unclear generality on some programmatically scored machine-learning tasks.

The measurement problem extends beyond judgment. METR is concerned that containerized evaluations may resemble the reinforcement-learning environments used to train models, potentially overstating real-world capabilities as similar environments become common in training.

Lifecycle Cost is a rough, model-estimated proxy for developing a containerized task environment and running and scoring it 100 times, rather than a direct estimate of an AI developer’s training-environment costs. After controlling for task length, METR found the higher-cost subset was 2.9 times as expensive as the lower-cost subset on average, while models performed 2.9 times worse by time horizon, equivalent to 1.5 doublings. Models nevertheless improved at similar rates on the two subsets, so the data associates cost with difficulty without showing slower progress on costlier tasks.

Industry observers note that METR reports no strong overall acceleration or deceleration across the tested public frontier on its separate METR Capability Index, which summarizes model performance on a common scale. Developer-specific slope changes were sensitive to methodological choices, leaving their validity uncertain.

METR nevertheless states current public evidence is insufficient to rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration in the next couple of years, defined as capabilities improving so swiftly that humans can no longer meaningfully understand, assess and react to catastrophic risks from latest systems. Which capabilities would produce that outcome remains unknown, and easy-to-verify tasks alone might suffice. The findings therefore make weaker judgment a plausible constraint on research automation, not proof that acceleration must wait for models to perform well on realistic tasks associated with ordinary jobs.

In a recent development, jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

Recent findings suggest that with a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI on November 20, 2026 revealed stronger defenses against adversarial distillation, reporting that the average success rate for adaptive attacks extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request fell from 54.0% on GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% on GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards.

Industry observers note that for extraction from the current request, the corresponding average fell from 22.9% to 0.9%, OpenAI reports. The adaptive black-box evaluation aggregates results across six attacker models, with automated red-teamers adjusting their approach as the system responds and seeing only what an external user would see. The strengthened protections cover GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and selected improvements are also being applied to GPT-6 Astra.

Protected reasoning is the intermediate chain-of-thought a model generates while working toward an answer. These traces can contain information omitted from final responses, making them especially valuable to adversarial distillation, which uses a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another system. The resulting model may reproduce dual-use capabilities without the safeguards that constrained the original.

OpenAI’s internal study compared two training runs from the same pretrained student model, the learner in a setup where a teacher model produces the training data. One run used exact teacher reasoning traces; the other used the user-visible baseline of final responses, reasoning summaries and tool interactions. The fine-tuning data consisted primarily of Astra-level teacher trajectories on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Students were evaluated after supervised fine-tuning and again after lightweight reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

Recent findings suggest that after supervised fine-tuning, the exact-trace student generally outperformed the summary-trained student, OpenAI reports. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student scored higher at the largest tested inference budget on both reported benchmarks, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.

It has been revealed that openAI interprets the results as evidence that protecting exact traces can limit cyber-capability transfer even when the underlying tasks are permitted under its usage policies, while saying it will continue studying transfer across different student models and training recipes. Across many such interactions, exact traces can teach skills that generalize beyond the teacher’s original tasks.

In a recent development, at the request level, adversarial training teaches models to recognize extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning while preserving legitimate explanations and assistance. Input classifiers look for extraction attempts, while output classifiers inspect assistant messages and tool-call arguments in streaming and non-streaming responses. Tool-call coverage matters because reasoning can appear in a tool’s arguments without appearing in the final answer; output classifiers can block suspected leaks before they reach the caller.

Sources indicate that the updated API ties protected reasoning in GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to the conversation history that produced it. A model can build on earlier reasoning as messages are added, but rewriting an earlier message drops the reasoning that followed it. Older model families with weaker safeguards cannot read the two models’ protected reasoning, restricting reuse across model-family boundaries.

Campaign-level defenses use request and account signals to investigate coordinated extraction, and attacks uncovered during investigations become examples for safeguard training and testing. OpenAI noted weekly enforcement actions against unauthorized distillation campaigns in 2026 have ranged from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly during summer 2026. The company tracks abuse prevalence and detection-to-enforcement time, aiming to reduce the data attackers obtain, raise campaign costs and shorten response times.

The announcement follows OpenAI’s September 30, 2026 disclosure of a coordinated campaign first observed on July 1, 2026. The earlier report described 16,000 attempted extraction requests from more than 4,000 consumers on July 24 and 25, 2026, attributed a core cluster to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, and said it was unclear whether all operators belonged to one actor.

OpenAI shares indicators of compromise with other model providers and works with deployment partners on safeguard requirements and coordinated enforcement. Its recommendations for other developers include checking assistant messages and tool-call arguments, restricting encrypted-reasoning reuse across conversations and models, retaining successful attacks as regression tests for future safeguards, and pairing request controls with campaign investigations. The tech giant plans to share more about recently disrupted campaigns.

It has been revealed that openAI has told Congress it supports the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act and the MATCH Act, alongside broader legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors illicitly extracting capabilities from American AI models.

The company argues that export controls and distillation defenses address different parts of that risk: export controls limit access to hardware needed to train frontier models, while distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained.

For model providers, the practical security boundary extends beyond final answers to how reasoning is reused across conversations, exposed through tool calls and monitored across accounts. The study also suggests that permitted coding and defensive-cybersecurity tasks can create a capability-transfer risk, making interaction-wide protection and campaign enforcement parts of the same defense.

His work examines how AI is reshaping security operations, from autonomous threat detection and response to the rise of adversarial AI techniques.

Sources indicate that with a technical and investigative perspective, Miles analyzes security research, incident disclosures, and real-world deployments to understand where AI strengthens defenses—and where it introduces new vulnerabilities. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Custom kernels are the backbone of high-performance deep learning, enabling GPU operations tailored precisely to your workload; whether that’s image processing, tensor transformations, or other compute-heavy tasks.
  • In this guide, we focus exclusively on ROCm-compatible kernels and show how to build, test, and share them using kernels.
  • This ROCm-specific walkthrough is a streamlined version of the original kernel-builder guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Custom kernels are the backbone of high-performance deep learning, enabling GPU operations tailored precisely to your workload; whether that’s image processing, tensor transformations, or other compute-heavy tasks. But compiling these kernels for the right architectures, wiring all the build flags, and integrating them cleanly into PyTorch extensions can rapidly become a mess of CMake/Nix, compiler errors, and ABI issues, which is not fun. Hugging Face’s kernels library makes it easy to build (with kernel-builder) and share these kernels with the kernels-community, with support for multiple GPU and accelerator backends, including CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and XPU. This ensures your kernels are fast, portable, and seamlessly integrated with PyTorch.

In this guide, we focus exclusively on ROCm-compatible kernels and show how to build, test, and share them using kernels. You’ll learn how to create kernels that run efficiently on AMD GPUs, along with best practices for reproducibility, packaging, and deployment.

This ROCm-specific walkthrough is a streamlined version of the original kernel-builder guide. If you’re looking for the broader CUDA-focused version, you can find it here: A Guide to Building and Scaling Production-Ready CUDA Kernels.

We will use the GEMM kernel from RadeonFlow_Kernels as an example. If you want to go straight to the guide, click here.

This section was written by the RadeonFlow GEMM kernel authors to introduce the kernel.Authors: ColorsWind, Zesen Liu, and Andy.

The RadeonFlow GEMM kernel is a high-performance, FP8 block-wise matrix multiplication implementation optimized for the AMD Instinct MI300X GPU. GEMM (General Matrix Multiplication) is the core building block behind most deep learning workloads: given two matrices A and B, you compute their product C = A × B. Here it’s implemented in FP8, a low-precision floating-point format that trades a bit of accuracy for much higher throughput and lower memory bandwidth. This kernel was developed for the AMD Developer Challenge 2025, it was awarded the 🏆 Grand Prize in June 2025, recognizing its excellence in performance and innovation on AMD hardware.

In a recent development, the kernel operates on quantized inputs using the e4m3fnuz floating-point format and applies per-block scaling to preserve accuracy during low-precision computation. The e4m3fnuz format is an FP8 variant with 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, designed to be efficient for neural network workloads. Because FP8 has a much smaller dynamic range than FP16/FP32, we apply per-block scaling factors (a_scale and b_scale) so that each block of values is rescaled into a numerically “comfortable” range before and after computation, which helps preserve accuracy despite the low precision. It takes the following arguments:.

where a and b are the input matrices, a_scale and b_scale are the scaling factors for a and b respectively, and c is the output matrix:.

The kernel is precompiled for specific matrix shapes and assumes a transposed memory layout (as required by the competition). To support additional shapes or alternative memory layouts, you must modify the kernel launcher.

This is a fairly technical guide, but you can still follow it step by step without understanding every detail and everything will work fine. If you’re curious, you can always come back later to dig deeper into the concepts.

Thinking Machines Lab Releases Inkling 2 Mini for Local Devices

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops.
  • Industry observers note that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face.
  • A company demonstration demonstrates Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops. It has 26.4 billion total parameters and a memory footprint of about 20GB, using repeated passes through its middle layers to improve reasoning.

Industry observers note that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face. Tinker offers inference and fine-tuning, with chat in Tinker Playground, while local options include Ollama on Mac systems with at least 32GB of RAM and GGUF versions through Unsloth and llama.cpp.

A company demonstration demonstrates Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes. Another demonstration uses one offline MacBook to power all 20 residents of Thinkyville, a simulated pixel town, illustrating how multiple persistent agents can run locally.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer, meaning only a subset of its specialized components is used for each token. Its 24 layers are divided into four blocks of six. The first and last blocks run once, while the two middle blocks share weights and run three times, producing 48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers. The model has 3.4 billion active parameters and 5.4 billion weight activations per token once looping is included.

Sources indicate that attention residuals let each layer learn its own mixture of earlier block outputs instead of adding every output into a single running sum. The second and third passes also receive a gated message from the preceding pass. That gate initially blocks the message and learns to admit more of it during training, allowing looping to be introduced without destabilizing the model.

In the company’s training comparison, an unpruned non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512,000-token agentic traces.

Training began with 384 experts and eight selected per token. Two-thirds were pruned during midtraining, leaving the 128 most-used experts in each layer, after which the model trained on 1 trillion tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model to recover its earlier performance. Twenty layers were trained and are deployed in 4-bit NVFP4, with the final four in 8-bit MXFP8; the organization notes matching training and deployment precision avoids conversion loss from post-training quantization.

Thinking Machines Lab reports scores of 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 77.9% on the 51-task SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard evaluation, compared with 42.2% and 73.8% for Qwen3.8-27B, respectively, alongside 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2. Its comparison notes that evaluation setups vary by model.

The manufacturer claims looping improves reasoning without enabling the weights to store more facts; knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s AA-Omniscience result is in line with other models of its size, while its leads among similar-sized open-weights models on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA and MCP Atlas come from efficient use of search and tools.

The company also says Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or instructions with many constraints, reporting 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1. It trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks including CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

It has been revealed that looping complicates chain-of-thought monitoring, the practice of reading a model’s written reasoning to oversee its behavior. A conventional transformer must externalize reasoning that needs additional sequential steps; a looped model can perform more of those steps internally before producing text. Reasoning that never enters the text cannot be inspected by that kind of monitor.

Industry observers note that because Inkling 2 Mini supports only a fixed number of passes, the lab trained TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five passes, mostly three, and conducted reinforcement learning at three. On a Think Fast subset, the firm reports that its no-chain-of-thought time horizon, defined as the human completion time of tasks it can finish at 50% reliability without written reasoning, rose from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three before roughly flattening. N-Hop Lookup accuracy continued improving through ten loops even though training had not exceeded five passes.

In the tech giant’s initial analysis of GPQA Diamond questions answered correctly at every tested depth, average reasoning traces fell from 3,703 tokens at one pass to 1,661 at five. Mean sentence length changed only from 8.9 to 8.7 words, and the share of words found in an English dictionary moved from 94.6% to 94.4%; the shorter traces were more direct and involved less backtracking.

Industry observers note that the agentic tests used a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-loop model in LinuxArena. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as a weaker monitor, the organization found no clear trend in stealth rate as loop count increased; restricting the monitor to tool calls and outputs left a significant number of attacks undetected.

These monitorability results are preliminary. Reinforcement learning only at three passes means the experiments do not establish what a model trained at higher pass counts would learn, and the company cautions that such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively.

For oversight researchers, the open question is whether the legibility observed at this scale survives larger models and training regimes that optimize deeper loops. The fixed and variable open-weights releases provide a direct way to investigate that question across looping depths.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bot-based buying is here or not, depending on where you stand in the Amazon empire.

Sources indicate that amazon is of two minds when it comes to automated purchasing. The ecommerce giant has been busy banning AI shopping agents from accessing its website. Meanwhile, AWS Marketplace has opened its door to bot-based buying.

"Buying software and data through AWS Marketplace just got easier, for you and for the AI agents working alongside you," stated Mya Papolu, product marketing manager for AWS Marketplace and Partner Services at Amazon Web Services, in a blog post this week. "For re:Invent 2026, we’re launching capabilities designed to reduce friction across the buying journey.".

For a organization that has blocked bots from Google, Meta, and OpenAI, and sued Perplexity to keep its AI-encumbered Comet browser away, the openness of AWS Marketplace to agentic commerce invites questions.

We asked Amazon to explain but we've not heard back.

AWS Marketplace is allowing AI agents to scour its site and buy some cloud software products using the x402 agentic payment protocol, which is supported by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments.

According to recent reports, introduced by Coinbase and Cloudflare, x402 got handed over to the Linux Foundation earlier this year, and now has support from a variety of tech platforms, including AWS, Google, Stripe, and various blockchain networks. About a week ago, Brave Software declared support for x402 payments through its search API.

Industry observers note that AWS requires sellers to register with AWS Marketplace and to integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK to enable agentic product purchases. Transactions settle in USD through AWS billing so existing spending controls can be applied.

And now, customers in the US can buy some AWS Marketplace software without an AWS account; instead they're asked to provide an email or social media login, and a credit card.

Apriel-H1: The Surprising Key to Distilling Efficient Reasoning Models

📅 19 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss.
  • Industry observers note that when MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise.
  • Sources indicate that our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss. The key? A non-obvious insight about what data to distill on, and why intuition fails here.

Industry observers note that when MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise. The real lesson: it depends on your constraints.

Sources indicate that our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over. No infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. No luxury of architectural co-design from day one. Just a practical question: can you retrofit efficiency into an existing model through distillation?

Spoilers: yes, but only if you ignore your intuition about what data to use.

The Apriel-H1 family: seven checkpoints spanning 25-40 Mamba layers (out of 50 total), showing the complete efficiency-quality frontier. Our flagship Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT achieves 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss: MATH500 and MTBench improve a few points (0.90 → 0.92 and 8.30 → 8.58, respectively), while GSM8k (0.97 → 0.95), GPQA (0.59 → 0.55), and AIME24 (0.70 → 0.65) regress slightly. Total training: 76.8B tokens.

Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT (green) vs full-attention teacher (blue). Reasoning quality stays nearly flat across benchmarks while throughput increases 1.89-2.09x depending on context length.

The full details are in our Apriel-H1 paper. Here, we focus on the key insight that made it work.

Here's what we initially thought would work: just distill on pretraining data and round it out with some SFT.

Industry observers note that the reasoning seemed solid. We're inserting completely fresh Mamba layers that have never seen data. These linear SSMs need to learn general-purpose token mixing from scratch. How can they become effective mixers unless they get exposure to the same broad distribution the original attention layers saw?

So we tried it. Then we tried mixing pretraining and SFT data. It didn't work. The distilled hybrids lost reasoning quality, sometimes dramatically.

What actually worked: high-quality reasoning traces from the teacher's SFT dataset.

Distilling a reasoning model isn't about transferring general next-token prediction. The base model already has that, and we started from a strong 15B foundation. What we're preserving is specific and fragile: the teacher's multi-step reasoning patterns.

Industry observers note that those patterns emerge from intricate attention mechanisms. Retrieval heads pulling context from thousands of tokens back. Induction heads recognizing and continuing logical chains. Long-range dependencies connecting premises to conclusions many steps later. When you replace attention wholesale with Mamba's linear recurrence, these computational mechanisms are disrupted. The hybrid must discover newly introduced paths to the same reasoning outcomes.

That discovery requires explicit examples where reasoning structure is visible and correct:.

Pretraining data, on the other hand, is too noisy and too diffuse. The reasoning signal gets lost. You need concentrated examples of the specific capability you're trying to preserve.

Once we understood the data choice, our distillation method became clear too. We used reverse KL divergence (temperature 1) rather than forward KL. Reverse won consistently. Why? We're training on problems where the teacher has high confidence and clear structure. Reverse KL's mode-seeking behavior encourages the student to commit to those high-confidence predictions. When your teacher is confident and correct, you want your student to be confident too.

This insight is the key to the whole approach: match your distillation data to the capability you're preserving, not the capability you're building.

Industry observers note that you can't just swap 40 attention layers for Mamba and hope. We learned this the hard way, and eventually developed a staged distillation procedure to get there reliably.

It has been revealed that stage 1: Identify least-crucial layers. We used a Leave-One-Out (LOO) analysis on MMLU: remove each layer, replace with identity, then measure the drop. Sort by importance, replace the bottom 25 with Mamba-in-Llama (MIL) initialized mixers. Distill end-to-end. This worked for our H-25 checkpoint.

It has been revealed that stage 2: Progressive conversion beyond 25 layers. LOO broke down past 25 layers because layers unimportant in isolation became critical in combination. To address this, we developed a dynamic heuristic we call MIL-Mamba-Replacement (MMR). For each remaining attention layer, we initialize a Mamba mixer with MIL, run 100 training steps, and record the distillation loss. Layers converging to lower loss are "easier" to replace. This captures training dynamics rather than static importance.

We progressed incrementally: 25 → 27 → 30 → 34 → 37 → 40 Mamba layers, grouping replacements by MMR scores. Each checkpoint distills from the previous.

Stage 3: End-to-end training on SFT data. After reaching the target Mamba layer count, we did a final SFT pass until reasoning performance stabilized. After 55.9B distillation tokens and 20.9B SFT tokens, this produced our final Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT model.

According to recent reports, the complete efficiency frontier. Each checkpoint shows cumulative training tokens. Our flagship H-30-SFT (released as Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT) used 76.8B total for 2.1x throughput at 0.76 average score. The aggressively converted H-40 variant used 136.5B tokens for 3.4x throughput. For reference: NVIDIA's Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 achieves 4.6x at 0.77 score but required training from scratch with orders of magnitude more compute.

In a recent development, we built all this on Fast-LLM, our open-source training framework. The core architectural principle: large language model transformers should be modular. Attention and Mamba are different implementations of the same "mixing" interface, and can be swapped freely.

Here's a hybrid architecture in Fast-LLM's config format:.

The pattern field specifies layer order. For Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT: 30 mamba_block, 20 attention_block, placed by importance. That's it.

Distillation is configuration too:.

According to recent reports, fast-LLM handles gradient accumulation, distributed training, tensor parallelism, checkpointing, everything you need for large-scale experimentation. It's open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0. You can reproduce this work because we designed the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Sources indicate that why release all checkpoints? Because optimal depends on your constraints. H-30 offers the best balance. H-40 maximizes throughput for latency-critical workloads. The intermediate checkpoints let you choose your exact trade-off.

Sources indicate that why do you get different speedups at different context lengths? Mamba's linear complexity advantage grows with sequence length, and attention degrades quadratically.

Sources indicate that why did you only try Mamba? We used Mamba-1 for three reasons: it has a proven distillation track record, has shown strong empirical performance, and was simple to implement in our framework. It let us focus on the data question first.

What were the Mamba hyperparameters? State size 16, DT rank 16, inner dimension 4096. For our GQA setup in Apriel we expanded B (input projection) and x (state) to match total attention heads following M1.

Why didn't you try more advanced conversion methods? We used Mamba-in-Llama initialization and knowledge distillation rather than MOHAWK's multi-stage procedure because the latter didn't show significant advantages in preliminary experiments.

Why did you only SFT the H-30 model? We only applied SFT to H-30 to validate that distilled hybrids can be improved through standard post-training. The other checkpoints are pure distillation but can be fine-tuned similarly.

According to recent reports, why didn't you explore RL? This was a scoping decision to isolate the distillation question: can you transfer reasoning via knowledge distillation alone? Answer: yes. But RL should close remaining quality gaps further. We are exploring RL for future iterations.

According to recent reports, did you really show that Apriel-H1 matches full-attention reasoning at similar compute budgets? We didn't do an apples-to-apples comparison between full-attention Apriel and a hybrid trained identically from pretraining forward. That would require repeating all mid-training and post-training of the teacher with the Apriel-H1 architecture, which was beyond our compute budget. What we can claim though is that retrofitting efficiency via distillation is practical and effective, and that the resulting hybrids can be fine-tuned to match or exceed the teacher's reasoning quality.

Industry observers note that we've implemented Apriel-H1 in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM. Transformers integration is straightforward. We ship a new model class with interchangeable attention and Mamba layers. vLLM integration uses their recent Mamba cache operations for continuous batching, prefix caching, and chunked prefill. The vLLM plugin is ready. We are right now waiting for final legal approval to open-source it.

Recent findings suggest that honest assessment: Deploying hybrids today means rough edges. The tooling is maturing fast but isn't turnkey. You will write custom code, validate numerical behavior carefully, and work around framework limitations. For teams that can absorb that cost, throughput gains are worth it. For those that can't, waiting might be the right call.

According to recent reports, most teams don't have infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. If you've invested in a strong base model and need efficiency gains, this work reveals a practical path: distill into hybrids using high-quality task-specific data that matches the capability you're preserving.

Industry observers note that the surprising finding, use reasoning data to distill reasoning, seems obvious in retrospect but contradicts initial intuition. We validated it, explained why it works, and built the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Models: Apriel-H1 Collection on HuggingFaceTraining framework: Fast-LLM on GitHubTeacher model: Apriel-Nemotron-15B-ThinkerPaper: Apriel-H1: Towards Efficient Enterprise Reasoning Models.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
  • Recent findings suggest that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
  • Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Recent findings suggest that energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Server stamps encode all the parameters required to connect to a secure DNS server as a single string. Think about stamps as QR code, but for DNS.

Stamps can be rapidly viewed/modified/created using this VueJS component.

An online demo is accessible here: https://stamps.dnscrypt.info.

An example list of public secure DNS resolvers, with their DNS stamps.

0x01 is the protocol identifier for DNSCrypt.

Industry observers note that props is a little-endian 64 bit value that represents informal properties about the resolver. It is a logical OR combination of the following values:.

For example, a server that supports DNSSEC, stores logs, but doesnât block anything on its own should set props as the following 8 bytes sequence: [ 0x05, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00 ].

According to recent reports, addr is the IP address, as a string, with a port number if the server is not accessible over the standard port for the protocol (443). IPv6 strings must be included in square brackets: [fe80::6d6d:f72c:3ad:60b8]. Scopes are permitted.

pk is the DNSCrypt providerâs Ed25519 public key, as 32 raw bytes.

providerName is the DNSCrypt provider name.

Recent findings suggest that addr is the IP address of the server. It can be an empty string. In that case, the host name will be resolved to an IP address using another resolver.

hashi is the SHA256 digest of one of the TBS certificate found in the validation chain, typically the certificate used to sign the resolverâs certificate. Multiple hashes can be provided for seamless rotations.

In a recent development, hostname is the server host name which will also be used as a SNI name. If the host name contains characters outside the URL-permitted range, these characters should be sent as-is, without any extra encoding (neither URL-encoded nor punycode). The port number is optional, and is assumed to be 443 if missing.

path is the absolute URI path, such as /dns-query.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It isn't only systems on Earth suffering technical problems.

It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week.

Recent findings suggest that for Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications problem that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century.

In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters.

Industry observers note that earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain.

Recent findings suggest that more bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt.

In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth.

The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode.

Recent findings suggest that so far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output.

Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the problems – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold.

Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®.

LLMs have become essential tools for building software. But for Apple developers, integrating them remains unnecessarily painful.

Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:.

In a recent development, each comes with different APIs, different requirements, different integration patterns. It's a lot, and it adds up promptly. When I interviewed developers about building AI-powered apps, friction with model integration came up immediately. One developer put it bluntly:.

I thought I'd quickly use the demo for a test and maybe a quick and dirty build but instead wasted so much time. Drove me nuts.

The cost to experiment is high, which discourages developers from discovering that local, open-source models might actually work great for their use case.

Today we're announcing AnyLanguageModel, a Swift package that provides a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework with support for multiple model providers. Our goal is to reduce the friction of working with LLMs on Apple platforms and make it easier to adopt open-source models that run locally.

The core idea is simple: Swap your import statement, keep the same API.

Recent findings suggest that here's what that looks like in practice. Start with Apple's built-in model:.

Now try an open-source model running locally via MLX:.

AnyLanguageModel supports a range of providers:.

Recent findings suggest that the focus is on local models that you can download from the Hugging Face Hub. Cloud providers are included to lower the barrier to getting started and to provide a migration path. Make it work, then make it right.

It has been revealed that when designing AnyLanguageModel, we faced a choice: create a new abstraction that tries to capture everything, or build on an existing API. We chose the latter, using Apple's Foundation Models framework as the template.

According to recent reports, this might seem counterintuitive. Why tie ourselves to Apple's choices? A few reasons:.

Sources indicate that foundation Models is genuinely well-designed. It leverages Swift features like macros for an ergonomic developer experience, and its abstractions around sessions, tools, and generation map well to how LLMs actually work.

It's intentionally limited. Foundation Models represents something like a lowest common denominator for language model capabilities. Rather than seeing this as a weakness, we treat it as a stable foundation (hyuk hyuk). Every Swift developer targeting Apple platforms will encounter this API, so building on it directly means less conceptual overhead.

It keeps us grounded. Each additional layer of abstraction takes you further from the problem you're actually solving. Abstractions are powerful, but stack too many and they become a problem in themselves.

The result is that switching between providers requires minimal code changes, and the core abstractions remain clean and predictable.

Sources indicate that one challenge with multi-backend libraries is dependency bloat. If you only want to run MLX models, you shouldn't have to pull in llama.cpp and all its dependencies.

Sources indicate that anyLanguageModel uses Swift 6.1 package traits to solve this. You opt in to only the backends you need:.

Available traits include CoreML, MLX, and Llama (for llama.cpp / llama.swift). By default, no heavy dependencies are included. You get the base API plus cloud providers, which only require standard URLSession networking.

For Xcode projects (which don't yet support trait declarations directly), you can create a small internal Swift package that depends on AnyLanguageModel with the traits you need, then add that package as a local dependency. The README has detailed instructions.

Recent findings suggest that vision-language models are incredibly capable and widely used. They can describe images, extract text from screenshots, analyze charts, and answer questions about visual content. Unfortunately, Apple's Foundation Models framework doesn't right now support sending images with prompts.

According to recent reports, building on an existing API means accepting its constraints. Apple will likely add image support in a future release (iOS 27, perhaps?), but vision-language models are too useful to wait for. So we've extended beyond what Foundation Models offers today.

Here's an example sending an image to Claude:.

It has been revealed that we're taking a calculated risk here; we might design something that conflicts with Apple's eventual implementation. But that's what deprecation warnings are for. Sometimes you have to write the API for the framework that doesn't exist yet.

To see AnyLanguageModel in action, check out chat-ui-swift, a SwiftUI chat application that demonstrates the library's capabilities.

In a recent development, it's meant as a starting point: Fork it, extend it, swap in different models. See how the pieces fit together and adapt it to your needs.

Recent findings suggest that anyLanguageModel is presently pre-1.0. The core API is stable, but we're actively working on bringing the full feature set of Foundation Models to all adapters, namely:.

According to recent reports, this library is the first step toward something larger. A unified inference API provides the scaffolding needed to build seamless agentic workflows on Apple platforms — applications where models can use tools, access system resources, and accomplish complex tasks. More on that soon. 🤫.

We'd love your help making this better:.

We're excited to see what you build 🦾.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs.
  • The research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes.
  • Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs. MIT revealed the work on November 20, 2026.

The research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes. Their paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences was published online on October 12, 2026, and appeared in the journal’s October 20, 2026, issue.

Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes. A neural network may match data over a short period and still fail when left to run: small errors can accumulate until its simulated values grow without limit, even though the real system remains bounded. That behavior can invalidate estimates of long-term statistics, a central goal of modeling dissipative chaotic systems.

The guarantee therefore concerns long-term bounded behavior rather than exact point-by-point forecasting far into the future. It seeks to preserve valid long-run statistics without suppressing the complicated variation that makes the system chaotic. As Azizan put it, “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.”.

The framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator, which predicts how the system evolves, and an energy-like representation. That representation is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint inside a projection layer, which adjusts the model’s predicted evolution. Outside a learned boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing trajectories toward the bounded region while allowing chaotic behavior within it.

The paper indicates this construction enforces dissipation by design and provides formal trajectory-boundedness guarantees over arbitrarily long forecast windows. The learned energy boundary also supplies an outer estimate of the system’s strange attractor, whose complex geometry makes it difficult to characterize directly.

Tang mentioned soft penalties or incentives applied during training need not hold when a deployed model faces newly introduced inputs, so unbounded predictions remain possible. Arbitrary caps can keep outputs within a chosen limit, but they can also restrict the model’s ability to represent complex features that should be learned from data. The projection layer is modular and model-agnostic, allowing it to work with different neural-network architectures.

In a recent development, MIT reports that the approach closely tracked true outcomes in tests ranging from textbook systems to complex multidimensional cases, while conventional methods moved into impossible predictions. The published demonstrations include Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, where the method produced bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserved invariant statistics.

Industry observers note that A related Energy-Constrained Operator paper by Andrea Goertzen, Tang and Azizan was published on June 7, 2026. It introduced a closed-form quadratic projection layer and reported stable long-horizon forecasts that captured invariant statistics for systems governed by the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and Navier–Stokes equations. Both papers use control-theoretic energy conditions to tackle predictions whose unbounded growth prevents meaningful evaluation of long-run statistics.

Industry observers note that the algorithms and computer code have been deposited on GitHub, and the paper and open-source code are accessible online. The researchers hope other teams will build on the modular layer and test it on larger, more complex problems.

Recent findings suggest that the team plans to test progressively larger systems and data-driven models of realistic weather. Realistic-weather performance therefore remains an open research question: the immediate contribution is a formal limit on runaway simulations, while the next tests must establish how that guarantee affects the usefulness of models’ long-term statistics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic revealed on November 20, 2026 that it had closed a 1.127 billion-share Class A initial public offering at $83 per share, including underwriters’ full exercise of an option to buy 147 million additional shares. The IPO produced approximately $93.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

The final offering comprised 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 sold by certain selling stockholders. Approximately $91.6 billion of the gross proceeds went to Anthropic, which received no proceeds from the stockholders’ sales.

Anthropic’s November 18, 2026 pricing announcement had covered 980 million shares, including 956,351,354 from the organization, and granted underwriters a 30-day option for the additional shares. The selling-stockholder allocation remained unchanged when the option was exercised, so the full exercise expanded only Anthropic’s portion of the offering.

The final prospectus put the original offering’s aggregate price at $81.34 billion and stated that underwriters would receive no discount or commission on shares sold through the option. The higher final gross figure therefore reflects the additional shares rather than a change in the offering price.

According to recent reports, alongside the IPO, Anthropic closed the sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 per-share price to Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners. The private placement had an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. Together, the IPO—including the selling-stockholder shares—and the placement generated approximately $119.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

According to recent reports, the prospectus describes Class N holders as primarily strategic business partners. Each Class A share carries one vote, while Class N shares have no voting rights except where required by law. Class N shares generally convert into Class A when sold or transferred to an unaffiliated third party; Class A shares are not convertible.

In a recent development, the Class N sale was an unregistered private placement, and underwriters received no discounts or commissions on those shares. The placement shares were not subject to underwriter lock-up agreements, but they were restricted securities that could be resold only under an effective registration statement or an available exemption.

Anthropic’s Class A shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026. Official Nasdaq market data recorded a November 20 regular-session close of $88.91, down $8.26, or 8.50%, from the prior session’s $97.17 close. The session low was $83.05, just above the $83 offering price, leaving the stock above its IPO terms despite the day’s decline.

It has been revealed that the completed transactions give Anthropic substantial new capital and place nonvoting Class N shares with seven technology investors. Public Class A holders have a different position: their shares carry voting rights, but their value now moves with the market rather than the fixed IPO terms, as the second-session decline demonstrated.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other notable tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up latest ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other notable tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

Recent findings suggest that in a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the massive takeaways 👇.

In a recent development, models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

While highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

Industry observers note that for even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

That said, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for new dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

Industry observers note that for long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

The tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

Sources indicate that ⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what latest architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀.
