📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a upcoming adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

According to recent reports, multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

Recent findings suggest that MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

Industry observers note that rapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more rapidly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Sequential vs. Task Parallel vs. RapidFire AI: The adaptive scheduler maximizes GPU utilization across multiple configs and GPUs. The bottom row shows IC Ops in action—stopping, cloning, and modifying runs mid-flight.

AWS Routes HyperPod Inference Across Regions From One Endpoint

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions.
  • Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.
  • AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions. The service selects a cluster using capacity, queue, proximity and error signals, with automatic failover when a cluster becomes unavailable.

Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway. That cluster-level gateway continues to select individual model pods using signals including key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth; the new global tier selects the cluster first, while leaving pod selection unchanged.

AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere. In its example of four models served across five clusters in two Regions, per-model serving requires clients to track 20 endpoints. Cluster-level gateways cut that to five, while the global gateway provides one. The managed tier removes the need to build and maintain load balancers, DNS and cross-Region networking for this routing, and lets peak traffic overflow to clusters with available capacity.

Industry observers note that an operator publishes each participating cluster by enabling spec.globalRouting in its existing InferenceGatewayConfig, then calls CreateGlobalInferenceGateway with the clusters to group. Publishing creates a Network Load Balancer, a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service and certificate resources in the customer’s account. An unpublished cluster cannot be added successfully.

In a recent development, clients send OpenAI-compatible requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) to the regional endpoint. The gateway authenticates the caller and selects a healthy cluster, AWS PrivateLink carries the request within or across Regions, and the cluster’s Inference Gateway chooses the model pod. SageMaker operates the routing fleet, private endpoints, certificate validation, health checks, authentication and rate limiting; a service-managed publisher on each cluster supplies load metrics.

For each request, the gateway scores healthy clusters using four configurable signals:.

Customers overriding the defaults must set all four weights, using values from 0.0 to 1.0 that total 1.0, and can disable a signal with zero. UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway changes the weighting for fresh requests without reprovisioning, while in-flight requests finish under the old settings. AWS says workloads that prioritize resilience over proximity can raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity.

It has been revealed that the gateway health-checks every cluster and shifts traffic to the next-best cluster after a failure without requiring client changes, bringing a recovered cluster back gradually. A failed request is retried once on another cluster unless streaming has started; if no healthy cluster remains, the gateway returns HTTP 503. Adding a healthy cluster does not change the endpoint or disrupt other clusters, while removing one stops fresh requests but lets in-flight work finish.

Sources indicate that IAM separately controls standard and streaming invocation, and customer JSON Web Tokens, when used, travel inside the SigV4 signature. Requests reach clusters only over AWS PrivateLink, and AWS states that the gateway does not log or store prompts or completions. Deleting the global gateway stops its endpoint but leaves the per-cluster endpoints serving.

Bagelcode VP of AI Platform Jinhyung Park said in AWS’s announcement that beta tests routed requests across two Regions through the gateway and continued serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave the manufacturer’s small platform team cross-Region failover without building or maintaining its own routing layer.

The service is available in 13 Regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (N. California and Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London and Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo, Mumbai, Singapore and Sydney).

In a recent development, AWS advises single-cluster owners to remain on the cluster Inference Gateway endpoint and adopt the global service when adding a second cluster. Existing per-cluster endpoints continue serving during client migration, and a gateway containing only clusters in one Region can keep a workload there. A published cluster left outside any gateway receives no traffic even though its Network Load Balancer continues to run and incur charges.

By putting proximity, capacity and failure signals in one policy, the service makes the use of otherwise idle GPU capacity a configuration decision rather than a separate networking project.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • In a recent development, swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

In a recent development, swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks indicates much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that amazon Web Services rolled out managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console.
  • The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning.
  • Administrators can install, configure, patch and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amazon Web Services rolled out managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console. The first two extensions cover observability and user management, including directory integration.

The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning. HyperPod had already added API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based node setup, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management and deep health checks during 2026. Those features manage the cluster’s definition, capacity, network layout and hardware health; cluster extensions apply the same approach to node software that changes as research teams, monitoring requirements and package versions evolve.

Administrators can install, configure, patch and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK. HyperPod validates settings against the selected extension version’s schema before rollout and records the requested version and settings as the desired state. A node agent then applies only the components required by each node’s role, including on nodes added through scaling or replacement.

Sources indicate that updates submit only the settings being changed. HyperPod merges them into the stored configuration and restarts only affected components, without replacing nodes or rerunning lifecycle scripts. New extension versions can also be installed without an AMI enhancement. HyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema before rollout, and upgrades only move forward.

Industry observers note that each extension reports Creating or Updating during rollout, Active when every node runs the requested configuration without a reported problem, and Degraded when nodes fail or report problems. DescribeClusterExtension groups node-level health complications by cause with a code, message and affected-node count. HyperPod retries internal failures; administrators can correct other causes and retry affected nodes with an update call containing no configuration changes.

In a recent development, the sagemaker-observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Slurm job and Slurm cluster metrics, sending them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. Metric categories, levels and collection intervals are configurable, while nodes run only role-relevant components, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller.

In a recent development, an optional Amazon Managed Grafana workspace adds pre-created Clusters and Jobs dashboards. They connect cluster-wide health and Slurm state with per-node infrastructure metrics and resource use for individual jobs, including CPU, memory, GPU utilization, disk I/O and NCCL data.

Recent findings suggest that the sagemaker-user-management extension creates Linux people and groups with consistent IDs across nodes, controls SSH and passwordless sudo access by node type, and registers users with Slurm accounting. Accounts can be declared locally, drawn from Active Directory over LDAPS, or both, including connections to AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Fresh and replacement nodes receive the same configuration, and administrators can review access through the API instead of signing into each node.

In a recent development, cluster extensions require a HyperPod Slurm cluster using the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later, with continuous provisioning enabled. Because extensions run software as root, AWS treats create, revision and delete permissions as administrator permissions and advises against granting them to the cluster execution role. That role still needs access to metric destinations and Active Directory secrets, while user management requires a shared file system for home directories. Separate extension ARNs allow platform and monitoring teams to own different extensions.

Industry observers note that existing clusters can migrate one capability at a time while scripts and extensions coexist. The process requires updating the cluster software, disabling that capability in lifecycle scripts, manually removing script-installed agents during a maintenance window, and creating the extension on the clean cluster. Each component needs one owner: managing the same exporter, user or service through both mechanisms can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts remain available for organization-specific software, and administrators retain SSH and direct configuration access to every node, including the controller.

Industry observers note that both extensions are available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is supported. There is no additional charge for cluster extensions, but customers pay for underlying resources such as CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and AWS Secrets Manager.

It has been revealed that for shared foundation-model clusters, the operational consequence is that common node software becomes a declared, continuously checked part of cluster state rather than a collection of provisioning scripts. Removing script-installed agents is the one manual fleet-wide migration step; afterward, scale-ups and replacement nodes inherit the same extension settings, while organization-specific tooling remains under the cluster team’s control.

Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1429 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most crucial applications of AI.
  • According to recent reports, the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most crucial applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

According to recent reports, the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

According to recent reports, we learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

In a recent development, over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

Long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Industry observers note that using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

It has been revealed that ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

Industry observers note that at Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

Industry observers note that this approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these complications.

Sources indicate that A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

Sources indicate that from our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created new failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

We used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

In a recent development, rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

What is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

A great insight on getting more by doing less.

  • According to recent reports, the disclosure is an exploratory initiative, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anysphere, the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, told House investigators it looks to explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight AI models because of geopolitical risk, according to a joint congressional report released November 20, 2026.

According to recent reports, the disclosure is an exploratory initiative, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable. The House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China published the findings after an investigation that began in April 2026 and expanded from Airbnb and Anysphere to DoorDash on July 31, 2026.

Sources indicate that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship. The committees stated Composer 2, Cursor’s flagship proprietary model, was built on a Moonshot AI base whose identity became public only after an independent developer identified it.

Cursor’s technical report identifies that base as Kimi K2.5. Composer 2 underwent continued pretraining on a code-heavy data mix, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning in realistic Cursor sessions using the same tools and harness as the deployed model.

Recent findings suggest that airbnb reported that customized versions of Alibaba’s Qwen models support an AI assistant handling roughly 80,000 guest and host interactions daily, alongside a fine-tuned model summarizing roughly 250,000 support cases and calls each day. Both run on U.S.-based service-provider infrastructure.

Sources indicate that doorDash reported 25 Chinese model families authorized and deployed in a non-trivial manner, defined as incurring at least $5,000 in computing and serving costs. It estimated that replacing one Chinese-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, although most other uses could transition almost immediately.

The committees identified cost, customization, and near-frontier performance as adoption drivers, and found that the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

The report compares published API prices for one million input tokens and one million output tokens (small pieces of words and characters used to measure model usage):.

Those figures do not adjust for differences in capability, caching, batch discounts, promotions, or self-hosting costs. They illustrate the price pressure behind adoption, while open weights also let companies fine-tune models on their own data and deploy them on infrastructure they control.

In a recent development, the security concern is separate from hosting location. Running models on U.S. infrastructure reduces direct data exposure, but the report says that does not change how the underlying model was trained or how it may behave under conditions ordinary evaluations miss.

Industry observers note that the report’s 12 recommendations do not themselves enact restrictions. They would build on a Department of Homeland Security order excluding DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian procurement and requiring their removal from agency systems, including third-party products built on DeepSeek. The chairmen recommend extending those restrictions to other Chinese-developed models and their derivatives across federal information systems and federal contract work, with narrow waivers for research, testing, and defensive security. They also recommend barring those models and derivatives from narrowly defined high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, with removal schedules tied to trusted alternatives and temporary exceptions where no trusted substitute exists.

To make the rules enforceable, a model-provenance standard led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and a machine-readable AI bill of materials would document base models, significant fine-tuning, and distillation sources. The requirement would cover federal contractors and AI used in high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, and would be voluntary elsewhere. A national American open-weight AI initiative would combine public computing resources, shared evaluation infrastructure, voluntary licensing of American frontier-model outputs to qualified open-weight developers for training, and federal anchor demand.

Recent findings suggest that the committees warn that removing Chinese models before trusted open-weight alternatives exist could raise costs and concentrate the market among closed proprietary providers. Anysphere’s exploratory blueprint therefore illustrates the larger implementation test: restrictions need reliable lineage records to locate embedded models and credible substitutes to avoid trading Chinese open weights for higher costs or closed-model dependence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • Sources indicate that if you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
  • This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

Sources indicate that if you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one new token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many users simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

According to recent reports, the attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

This is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

Consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a upcoming conversation starts here.

Industry observers note that each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

Input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

We then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

In a recent development, finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

After applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

It has been revealed that furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

Recent findings suggest that for example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

The process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one new token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a fresh forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

Recent findings suggest that to compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

According to recent reports, this follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

According to recent reports, moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

Recent findings suggest that in the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

According to recent reports, let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

According to recent reports, KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

According to recent reports, up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

It has been revealed that let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

We can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the fresh KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

Industry observers note that in our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

Industry observers note that to batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the new token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

It has been revealed that where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

According to recent reports, the drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

At this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

But we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

Sources indicate that although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

In a recent development, in the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with upcoming chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

Industry observers note that by removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent customers efficiently.

In a recent development, in the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

Industry News: Verifying formal models of Raft implementations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.
  • At Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems.
  • In a recent development, in this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.

At Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems. But Antithesis can also help eliminate certain classes of bugs by using a combination of AI and formal methods to prove the correctness of complex design choices.

In a recent development, in this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp. Although theyâre implementing the same protocol, there are significant differences in the approaches the two use. We used AI, TLA+, and Antithesis to formally model the two libraries with trace validation. We iterated between model checking, Antithesis testing, and proof attempts, each of which exposed bugs in the code or gaps in the model. We patched bugs and refined the model until it was provable, and until every test run was conformant.

Our model handles several extensions to the core Raft algorithm including pre-votes, snapshots, leadership transfers, and, for etcd-raft only: read indexes for linearizability, async storage writes, and membership changes (where etcdâs implementation intentionally deviates from the Raft paper).

Sources indicate that the final proofs establish core Raft safety properties such as Election Safety, Leader Completeness, and State-Machine Safety. In other words, our process established that once we applied the workarounds and fixes needed, the specific designs (scoped to the features we modeled) embodied in HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft actually offer the same guarantees that the Raft paper does. We make the artifacts available for open review:.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, we wrote about how we keep finding bugs in every major Raft implementation we test with Antithesis. This was surprising, because the underlying Raft protocol has been extensively studied, formally specified, and rigorously proven correct (under a set of assumptions). In that post, we pointed out that many implementations subtly deviate from those assumptions, re-design the algorithm for performance, and/or extend the core Raft protocol with unverified extensions â thereby introducing bugs.

Sources indicate that since then, advances in AI have made automated theorem proving and formal verification of complex systems much more scalable, making it feasible to connect a specification to its implementation. So we set out to formally verify not just the core Raft protocol, but the specific designs implemented by production Raft libraries, incorporating custom data structures, different modes of concurrency, and various extensions such as pre-votes, leadership transfers, snapshots, and (in the case of etcd-raft) membership changes.

Recent findings suggest that A key challenge in applying formal methods is to identify a level of abstraction that both allows us to reason mathematically about desired properties, and bridges the gap between specification and implementation. We are not yet at the point of reasoning directly at the level of assembly instructions or even programming language semantics in order to verify distributed safety properties in production systems.

Both Anthropic/Theoremâs OSS-Verify and Google DeepMindâs AlphaProof Code only model single-threaded assembly code; whereas distributed systems are concurrent.

Recent findings suggest that the most widely used approach models the software as a state-transition system in a specification language such as TLA+, and checks invariants over these transitions for finite state spaces. TLA+ models can either be hand-written by experts, or these days, inferred directly from the code using AI. This approach has its own limitations, but is increasingly popular. The next challenge, then, is showing that the TLA+ model corresponds to the actual software that will run in production.

For our demonstration, we used Claude Fable 5.2 to automatically infer TLA+ models from the implementations of HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft and then manually reviewed the safety properties declared in the specifications.

Recent findings suggest that the etcd-raft repository has a TLA+ model crafted for trace validation that is now out of date, and is not designed for ease of proof. The Specular project produced models of etcd-raft and hashicorp-raft, but those models are designed for trace validation, not ease of proof, and the TLAPS leaderboard indicates that they remain unsolved as of 20 Nov 2026.

According to recent reports, we had to manually provide guidance on which features to model or leave out, what scenarios to specify for model checking, and make one refinement to the auto-generated safety properties. While AI is generally bad at inferring properties, in this case we simply instructed the agent to express the core safety properties defined in the Raft paper.

Thatâs where Antithesis helps.

Sources indicate that we used the recently launched Antithesis plugin to automatically set up a test cluster, an input-generating workload designed to handle all the features captured in the model, and assertions that correspond to the modelâs safety properties. The software was then tested under fault injection while being fed random inputs, exercising various code paths and thread / message interleavings.

Industry observers note that for this demonstration, we developed a lightweight trace validation kit that allowed the software running in Antithesis to emit structured log events that correspond to state transitions in the TLA+ specification. Any test execution that produced a trace that did not conform to some path in the model got flagged. A non-conformant trace could indicate incorrect instrumentation of the trace logging itself, or more seriously, a modeling error or a real bug in the system. We instructed our AI agent to diagnose which one of these it might be, using Antithesis as necessary, and continue iterating until the traces and the inferred model converged.

For both Raft models, the specification expresses the following safety properties, taken directly from the Raft paper:.

In a recent development, before trying to prove anything, we verified that these invariants hold on bounded instances using TLC, the standard TLA+ model checker. These instances, also synthesized by our AI agent, specify various bounds: clusters are usually three nodes, a single client value, at most a couple of terms of leader election, logs that are limited to a few entries, with only a handful of network messages in flight. These bounds sound tiny, but theyâre sufficient to create several interesting cases: competing elections, a deposed leader still replicating, log entries overwritten and re-replicated, crashes in the middle of an operation, etc. We also model checked various configurations of the Raft libraries, e.g. with pre-vote or snapshotting features enabled and disabled. These âsmallâ instances can reach a state space of over 1.6 million states, which TLC explores exhaustively. We also included some larger problems which were only checked via random simulation. If model checking triggered a safety violation, we attempted to reproduce it as an assertion failure locally or in Antithesis; if the software couldnât exhibit the behavior, the model had to be tightened.

Overall, our process was an iterative loop consisting of model checking (flagging invariant violations), trace validation (flagging deviations), model refinement (to fix design flaws or conformance), and software patching (to fix bugs).

Sources indicate that in some ways, this approach is similar to and inspired by Specular. However, given their goal of finding bugs, Specularâs approach involved using AI to identify buggy scenarios before writing models, which meant that static analysis was doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In contrast, our models are intended to be more general and prove safety of the full design.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, we encountered bugs in both systems, including previously known open challenges such as hashicorp/raft#695 and etcd-io/raft#551, as well as latest ones such as hashicorp/raft#746 and etcd-io/raft#558. In our internal repository, we applied a total of 7 patches across the two implementations. In each case, our goal was to make the system and model pass both verification and validation.

We also encountered a few additional crash bugs, but those donât violate safety.

In a recent development, but bounded model checking only demonstrates the absence of bugs in a small state space. The only way to get assurance for unbounded input sizes is via rigorous mathematical proof.

There are two good techniques for proving invariants correct for the whole specification: using a theorem prover integrated into TLA+ called TLAPS, or by translating the model into Veil, a library for the Lean proof assistant for modeling state-transition systems. We used both, delegating the task of proof construction to Claude Fable 5.2.

We used Veilâs official tla-to-veil LLM skill for the model translation, and the recommended approach of validating this via bounded equivalence checking, using TLC and Veilâs own model checker, on our previously stored instances.

In a recent development, ideally, a TLAPS proof provides the best assurance, since it can attest to safety properties defined on the TLA+ model itself. However, we decided to translate TLA+ to Veil and attempt proofs in Lean. Why? As described in the previous section, our process was extremely iterative, involving several steps of model refinement. We wanted to use the proof engine as additional feedback in that process, feeding it any candidate specifications on which bounded model checking and trace validation both succeeded. We found Leanâs interactive tactic paradigm, predictable performance, and persistent kernel-checked proof terms to be key benefits in this iterative process.

On one occasion, a model of etcd-raftâs membership change as implemented could not be proven correct, revealing a complex bug whose trigger was beyond the state space that bounded model checking explores. In such situations, we could use the Antithesis plugin to attempt to synthesize a workload to reproduce the counter-example.

According to recent reports, antithesis also helped in the proof construction process. When working on challenging parts of the proof, Claude hypothesized several intermediate invariants which if true would lead to a straightforward proof strategy. The agent then used Antithesis to promptly check if those invariants held true in test runs, and discarded them if run-time assertions failed. Antithesis thus made the proof construction phase more efficient.

It has been revealed that once we converged on a state where the safety properties were fully provable in Lean and the model was passing trace validation with Antithesis, we froze the specification and asked agents to prove the same invariants on the TLA+ spec directly with TLAPS. This last step wasnât strictly necessary, but eliminated any shadow of doubt concerning the Lean proofs and the TLA+ spec.

End-to-end, the work on each library cost less than $1,200 in Claude Fable tokens and approximately 2000 Antithesis compute-hours.

Less, we should note, than the prepaid allowance in a single month of Antithesis Teams.

Note that our final proofs verify formal models of the implementation, not the code itself. However, we can gain confidence about the modelâs fidelity based on the trace validation performed with the extensive test coverage that Antithesis provides, including fault injection such as network partitions and node crashes. To strengthen assurance even further, our iterative process involved several steps of mutation testing, including: mutating the specification to check that the proofs fall through, mutating stored test logs to ensure that trace validation fails, and mutating the software itself to ensure that everything breaks.

The models still make several assumptions about the environment, which limits the reach of verification. For example, both Raft libraries provide pluggable interfaces for local persistent storage. In our test workloads, we use BoltDB for storage and the models assume that no single write (e.g., a log entry or tuple of raft state) is ever torn or corrupted, which BoltDB guarantees. A crash can still fall between two writes.

It has been revealed that our work also leaves out several library features which we have not modeled, such as lease-based reads for etcd-raft (because it depends on wall-clock timing), async heartbeats for hashicorp-raft (because it is known to be very very buggy; really), and membership changes for hashicorp-raft (because we were exhausted from patching bugs in the simpler core). Finally, we only verify safety properties and ignore liveness in this prototype. A comprehensive list of assumptions and limitations is provided in the associated artifactâs README.

Given our reputation as âa fuzzing companyâ, formal methods might seem like an odd direction for us to explore. But we see ourselves less as âa fuzzing companyâ and more as a correctness company. We need a wide range of different approaches if we want to build truly robust systems. Each technique compensates for the weaknesses of the others. Moreover, they amplify each otherâs strengths. The first property-based testing framework, QuickCheck, derived test inputs from a functionâs static type. Many of our customers use both testing and formal methods, so we want to make the two techniques work better together.

The biggest weakness of formal specification is that it proves the design correct, but doesnât guarantee that the code we implemented actually matches the design. Trace validation uses the strengths of tests to compensate for the core weakness of formal specification. Validation works best if our tests can reach wildly unusual system states, which aligns well with our core technology.

Recent findings suggest that how formal specification can help testing is relatively less explored, but there are some opportunities here too. We often find that newcomers to property-based testing struggle to describe the properties for their system. But they can describe a high-level outline of what the system essentially does. With trace validation, we can potentially turn that outline into a property to test!

It has been revealed that all that noted, this is an early research project. We could easily map trace logs to spec behaviors because the code and spec were at roughly the same level of abstraction, with a close correlation between lines of Go and lines of TLA+. Most real-world specs, though, are two levels of abstraction above the code they model. This is because 1) TLA+ can do things impossible in a real system, like make truly arbitrary nondeterministic choices, and 2) the spec can simplify implementation details that donât affect the essential design. These features make specification more powerful, but also make trace validation harder.

Think of this as us demonstrating a medicine works on mice, but we havenât yet done a human trial. More work is needed, work which weâre now doing at Antithesis. Stay tuned to see where it ends up.

Sources indicate that in formal specification (like with TLA+), we write highly abstract blueprints, or specifications, of systems and find bugs in those blueprints directly. Once weâve found and fixed all the bugs, we can be confident our real system isnât going to have certain design problems.

But how do we know that the code we write actually corresponds to the design we verified? This is one of the major unsolved problems of formal specification, and the solution we used here trace validation (also called âtrace checkingâ). This was first publicly described in the MongoDB paper eXtreme Modeling in Practice. The authors took logged events in the production system, converted them into a sequence of states, and checked if that sequence was possible in the blueprint. If not possible, then the implementation must be doing something forbidden by the blueprint, so there is a divergence between the implementation and spec.

Itâs easier to see this with a concrete example. Say we have this pseudocode as our specification:.

Recent findings suggest that by either-or, I mean that exactly one of the two will happen each iteration, but the decision logic is an implementation detail I donât care about. This spec also has the property that, after every loop iteration, passed + failed == i.

Now hereâs one conforming implementation:.

It has been revealed that while the practical way this works is very different than just arbitrary incrementing variables, itâs still the same thing in essence, and we should expect that every sensor either gets added to the set or marked as broken. To do trace validation, we first add some logs to the code:.

In a recent development, we run this program and it prints âloop passed loop failedâ. We can convert that to a behavior of the spec. If we denote a state as (i, passed, failed), the corresponding sequence of states would be [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)]. That is valid under the behavior, so this trace conforms to the spec.

Now if we make a diverging change like this:.

According to recent reports, itâs now possible to run this and see the logs âloop loopâ. The corresponding behavior, [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)] is impossible in the spec, so this would fail trace checking and reveal a divergence between the code and spec.

Industry observers note that thatâs how it all works in principle, anyway. Thereâs a lot of technical challenges with getting this working practically. For example, how are we supposed to know that a network timeout may give us an invalid trace, and how are we actually supposed to trigger it? And the answer to that is a combination of the techniques that we use in Antithesis: deterministic simulation testing and fuzzing. But those are things that we talk about in detail in other articles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oracle noted in a November 20, 2026 statement that it had secured all funding required for its OpenAI infrastructure contract and described itself as the first hyperscaler fully funded for this investment cycle. The announcement followed what Oracle called its final capital raise earlier in November.

The financing outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Oracle called any further private discussions with vendors “additional options,” said delivery of the OpenAI contract does not depend on them, and preemptively characterized contrary media reports as incorrect.

Industry observers note that at its October 28, 2026 Investor Day, Oracle committed to limiting additional capital-market funding for its fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2030 investment cycle to $20 billion, excluding refinancing of existing debt. The expected split was $10 billion in equity and $10 billion in gross debt.

That amount was in addition to a $20 billion equity raise completed in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 through an at-the-market program, under which Oracle could sell shares over time at prevailing market prices. Vendor financing, customer-provided hardware, and customer prepayments were also expected to reduce upfront cash requirements during the transition to positive free cash flow.

Sources indicate that the framework followed Oracle’s February 1, 2026 financing initiative, which targeted $45 billion to $50 billion of gross cash proceeds during calendar 2026. The stated purpose was to build additional Oracle Cloud Infrastructure capacity for contracted demand from its largest customers, including OpenAI. Oracle planned to raise approximately half through equity-linked and common equity issuances and the other half through a single, one-time issuance of investment-grade senior unsecured bonds early in 2026.

Sources indicate that the equity portion was expected to include an initial issuance of mandatory convertible preferred securities and the at-the-market program. Oracle noted in February that it did not expect to issue additional bonds during calendar 2026 beyond the planned transaction.

According to recent reports, the Abilene campus, where Astra-6 was trained, is nearly complete. Shackelford, Oracle’s next gigawatt-scale campus, is fully permitted, and the tech giant stated handover of NVIDIA Vera Rubin racks in its data halls was “on track for the coming weeks.”.

Recent findings suggest that oracle continues to expect positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 and is targeting more than $30 billion in fiscal 2029, when it expects growth to become self-funded. Peak capital expenditure was expected in fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028, followed by a step-down in fiscal 2029.

In a recent development, oracle’s assurance addresses the availability of capital, while the infrastructure work and spending transition remain unfinished. Campus delivery and the planned reduction in capital expenditure are the milestones linking the funding announcement to the manufacturer’s goal of self-funded growth.

Baseten Extends Decision Models to 128K Context and Image Input

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Baseten released bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 20, 2026, two open-weight models post-trained from Google’s Gemma 4 to return calibrated probabilities for predefined decisions.
  • In a recent development, both are available through Baseten Model APIs and as weights on Hugging Face.
  • In a recent development, bison-1 is a dense 31B-parameter model post-trained from Gemma 4 31B.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Baseten released bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 20, 2026, two open-weight models post-trained from Google’s Gemma 4 to return calibrated probabilities for predefined decisions. Artificial Analysis scored bison-1 at 76 on Decision Index v2.1, placing it first among 19 evaluated decision models.

In a recent development, both are available through Baseten Model APIs and as weights on Hugging Face. They accept text and images and support 131,072 tokens; Baseten claims that is eight times the 16K context of its previous mammoth-1, elephant-1 and joey-1 APIs. A request can bundle one state and any number of yes/no, named-choice or ordered-score questions into one shared-prefix prefill, without generating text.

In a recent development, bison-1 is a dense 31B-parameter model post-trained from Gemma 4 31B. Groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model based on Gemma 4 26B-A4B, with about 4B active parameters per token. Baseten prices them at $0.10 and $0.035 per million tokens, respectively, matching mammoth-1 and elephant-1.

Both use the same API as Baseten’s earlier decision models, and requests above the trained length limits are rejected rather than truncated. Google’s Gemma 4 base models carry Apache License 2.0 terms; Baseten’s modifications are released under the MIT License, with use subject to both licenses.

The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 combines six evaluations conducted independently by Artificial Analysis. AA-Paperclip, covering decisions and extraction across 1,500 resumes, receipts, invoices and research papers, carries 30% of the weight. The When2Call tool-calling evaluation carries 10%, while tests of workplace judgement, knowledge and hallucination, reasoning and decision invariance each carry 15%.

Recent findings suggest that its Decision Score subtracts a Brier calibration penalty from accuracy. The underlying probabilities also support confidence thresholds that answer some cases and route others elsewhere, making calibration relevant to how a decision system is deployed.

Artificial Analysis’s November 19, 2026 results place d1.2-ultra second at 75 and mammoth-1 at 71, while bison-1’s 0.14 Brier score is the index’s lowest, against 0.15 for d1.2-ultra. The Brier measure calculates the mean squared gap between the probability assigned to the chosen answer and whether that answer is correct. Lower values indicate confidence that more closely matches actual outcomes.

The bison-1 model card reports first-place results on When2Call, EvalSafe-O*NET-AA, HLE-MultiChoice v1.1 and AA-Symmetry v1.1, plus second place on AA-Paperclip. Its 60 on AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1 ranked 11th, so the aggregate lead includes substantial variation across components rather than uniform dominance.

Groundhog-1’s model card states that it has not yet received an Artificial Analysis Decision Index score.

Both models were trained on 6.71 million decision examples spanning core decision skills, safety and abstention, judging and expert domains, documents and long-context tasks, including public benchmark sets. The objective combines cross-entropy with a Brier calibration term and includes a trained I don't know option. About one example in seven carries a probability target instead of a single right answer.

Industry observers note that baseten attributes a significant calibration gain to expanding these soft-label targets alongside the Gemma base. Training used 192 B200 GPUs for bison-1 and 128 for groundhog-1.

According to recent reports, in Baseten’s own long-context runs at 128K tokens, bison-1 scored 84.8 on LongMemEval M and 87.1 on LongMemEval S, while groundhog-1 scored 77.4 and 79.3, respectively. These company-run tests address long-context performance separately from Artificial Analysis’s broader six-part index.

The release extends long-context, multimodal decision making across both of Base Labs’ established price tiers. Groundhog-1’s independent index result remains the open question for judging whether its mixture-of-experts design delivers the mammoth-1-level performance Baseten expects.
