Latest Update: Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.
  • It has been revealed that FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely fresh model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

In a recent development, first, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

Industry observers note that FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

According to recent reports, none of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

According to recent reports, due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

Industry observers note that ⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

The example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:.

For GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

In a recent development, FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

In a recent development, FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

It has been revealed that being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Sources indicate that many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

#57693. Latest Update: Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2014 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • According to recent reports, today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

According to recent reports, today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

Recent findings suggest that this growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

For v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

The first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each fresh model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

It has been revealed that transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

Transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 upcoming models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

According to recent reports, over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

We give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

While we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for new model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

It has been revealed that we’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a upcoming model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

According to recent reports, we’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

We'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

With its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

In a recent development, -- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a massive focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

We continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, fresh APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

Similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two newly introduced APIs dedicated to inference:.

According to recent reports, we see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

The Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more users. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

Standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Recent findings suggest that recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

We've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

It has been revealed that finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Quantization is quickly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

In a recent development, we're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate upcoming quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

The overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

Version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

We took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

Awesome work, great job of maintaining the library, it sure isn't easy with all the different architectures and advancements.

Congratulations for the launch !

In a recent development, no, you don’t! It’s just pure control. Researchers would love to have direct PyTorch only access to the architecture, training, and inference code for different models without this Transformers blab.

We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • In a recent development, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • Sources indicate that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial shows you how it works and how to use it yourself.

In a recent development, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

Sources indicate that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

Hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

Recent findings suggest that let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

The coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

The open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

Sources indicate that this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

This is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

In a recent development, the skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an update:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

In a recent development, that's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

Recent findings suggest that the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

In a recent development, SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

According to recent reports, use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

For models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Industry observers note that use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

In a recent development, DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and demonstrates you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

It has been revealed that you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

In a recent development, the model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

For tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train quickly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

It has been revealed that for small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

For medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

In a recent development, always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

According to recent reports, dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

In a recent development, real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

This highlights training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

If something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

Sources indicate that after training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

We've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

The skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

According to recent reports, using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

Temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Sources indicate that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

Industry observers note that we benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

Industry observers note that we observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and indicates the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

DeepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

Executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

#57689. China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (986 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Darkreading ↗ Open Full Page

China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the last wave of major VMware vCenter security updates, a China-nexus threat group likely already had its next zero-day up its sleeve.
  • Chinese state-sponsored hackers have been using a newly disclosed VMware zero-day vulnerability and an array of custom malware to compromise victims' virtualization stacks for several months.
  • According to recent reports, in October, Mandiant described a campaign by China's Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the last wave of major VMware vCenter security updates, a China-nexus threat group likely already had its next zero-day up its sleeve.

Chinese state-sponsored hackers have been using a newly disclosed VMware zero-day vulnerability and an array of custom malware to compromise victims' virtualization stacks for several months.

According to recent reports, in October, Mandiant described a campaign by China's Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool. The group used a zero-day to breach the edge appliance, then stole credentials and secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. Exactly what that downstream compromise looked like, though, was unclear at the time.

It appears now that BeyondTrust was merely an entrée to a deeper, more interesting, and much more complex campaign. In a follow-up blog post this week, Mandiant researchers described a chained attack beginning with Beyond Trust, moving through obscure Linux appliances, and landing on VMware technologies, at which point the attackers utilized another zero-day and more than half a dozen malware programs to totally undress their targets' virtual machine (VM) environments.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Manufacturer Breached in 2 Days.

That zero-day has only now come to light, months since China first exploited it. In a security advisory, VMware owner Broadcom recommended that customers revision their systems. Tracked as CVE-2026-123890, the vulnerability allows for authentication bypass in VMware vCenter, and earned a "critical" 9.8 out of 10 score in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).

From tagged Remote Support boxes, Mandiant observed Armory Castle scanning a victim's internal environment, looking for open ports associated with VMware.

Instead of going for the goods immediately, the group established forward operating bases inside of other, possibly unrelated Linux appliances in the same network. These appliances lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) visibility, allowing the group to establish persistence and stage its malware arsenal away from the parts of the network where defenders were looking. Among other malware, it was there that Armory Castle deployed "Bonesaw," a Go-based remote exploitation tool customized for vCenter.

The VMware vCenter Server is the central control plane used to manage multiple VMs and their ESXi hosts. Because it oversees everything else, few technologies are more useful for lateral movement, ransomware attacks, etc. than vCenter is. It's why this summer, the disclosure of two critical vCenter vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310, caused a stir.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another.

While organizations were rushing to patch the two vCenter vulnerabilities known to Broadcom, Armory Castle appears to have had an extra one up its sleeve. In September, it was able to use Bonesaw against a victim that had already patched its vCenter; Bonesaw was tuned to exploit CVE-2026-123890, a flaw that stems from the vCenter login system's use of predictable, time-based UUIDv1 timestamp generation in Secure Remote Password (SRP) authentication handling.

It has been revealed that exploiting CVE-2026-123890 afforded Armory Castle a shared session key it could use to create latest authenticated sessions as an administrator, bypassing the normal authentication process entirely. Bonesaw then paid more dividends, automating the process of copying vCenter's internal directory database, and creating powerful new accounts for further damage.

At this point, Armory Castle had total control over the victim's vCenter. Yet it continued on with machine-like focus; the attackers deployed a tool called "Sawsnake" to turn the Bonesaw-stolen vCenter login-signing key into forged authentication tokens, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) and enabling impersonation of any user. It then jumped to ESXi hypervisors, and found and extracted system files.

For high-risk organizations, updating VMware instances to patched versions can't be the end of the story.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks.

Because vCenter is just so sensitive, Mandiant urged organizations not to rely solely on patching known vulnerabilities as they come up. It pointed to its vSphere Defender's Guide, published earlier this spring. Its recommendations include the standard fare — promptly updating and isolating management systems, encrypting particularly sensitive systems, and applying especially tight controls to administrator accounts — but also offers more pointed items. It notes that vCenter doesn't necessarily record all important operating system (OS) activity, and that sophisticated attackers can delete local logs post-compromise; therefore, organizations should consider forwarding logs to a separate security information and event management (SIEM) platform.

Industry observers note that mandiant researchers also advised that organizations not rely on vCenter's built-in firewall, as it has too many limitations. For example, it doesn't generate remote logs for rejected connection attempts or certain shell activity, doesn't enforce policies for data egress, and, most of all, it's simply at risk for being built into the very system it's designed to secure.

"Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities," the researchers wrote.

#57688. npm stopped taking weekends

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

npm stopped taking weekends

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For six years, npm had the same week.
  • Then in spring 2025 that started to go.
  • A weekend day's downloads as a share of a weekday's, npm and PyPI (the data).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For six years, npm had the same week. Five busy days, then a Saturday and Sunday at about a quarter of the pace, because the people running npm install were at work and then they weren't.

Then in spring 2025 that started to go. npm's downloads API has a daily total for the whole registry going back to 2015, so here's a weekend day as a share of a weekday, quarter by quarter, with PyPI beside it:.

A weekend day's downloads as a share of a weekday's, npm and PyPI (the data).

The median weekend day over the median weekday, each quarter. npm's from its downloads API, PyPI's from ClickHouse's public ClickPy data. Days npm reports as zero and the Christmas fortnight are left out, and 2026 Q4 runs to 19 November.

npm sat between 23% and 29% for 25 quarters in a row. It's at 47% now.

In a recent development, I was pulling those totals to see how substantial the AI boom looks from the registry's side, and the size is daft enough on its own. npm served 292 billion downloads in October 2024, 424 billion in October 2025 and just over a trillion this October.

Recent findings suggest that but a bigger registry with the same weekly shape would just be more of the same. The extra downloads since summer 2024 run at 54% on weekends, so whatever's adding them barely keeps office hours. That's close to PyPI, which has been up there as far back as the data goes.

Sources indicate that the obvious answer is all the latest apps AI tools are spinning up, installing whatever's in fashion. So I looked at packages nobody starts a project with any more.

Sources indicate that node-sass has been deprecated on npm since 2024, with a notice telling you to use sass instead. In summer 2024 it got about 286,000 downloads on a normal weekday and 62,000 on a weekend day. Now it's 155,000 and 82,000. Fewer people install it on a Tuesday than two years ago, and more do on a Saturday. TSLint, which told everyone to move to ESLint back in 2019, has nearly doubled at weekends with its weekdays flat. And left-pad, of all things, went from 21% to 59%.

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones, then and now (the data).

Summer 2024 is July to September, autumn 2026 is 1 October to 19 November. Medians, like the chart above.

Packages people still use moved just as much. When I checked 507 of the biggest on 14 November, 506 had gone up by at least 10 points, and none was still under 30%. Taking the biggest few hundred out of the registry's total leaves the line where it was, so it isn't a few giants dragging the average along.

Sources indicate that vaul is my favourite. It's a drawer component for React, and its README opens with "This repo is unmaintained". The last release was December 2024. In summer 2024 it got 76,000 downloads a weekday, and now it gets 5.4 million, because the Radix version of shadcn/ui's drawer is built on it, and AI app builders like Lovable start you off with the whole shadcn set. Lovable also puts its own Vite plugin, lovable-tagger, in the projects it makes, and of the 76,416 package.json files on GitHub that list it, 75,904 list vaul too.

So who's installing node-sass on a Saturday? A download count doesn't say who asked for it, but packages with a separate binary for each platform give a hint. esbuild ships one for Linux, one for Macs, one for Windows and a pile of others, and npm only fetches the one for the machine it's running on.

Linux stopped taking weekends before Macs and Windows did (the data).

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones for @esbuild/linux-x64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64 and @esbuild/win32-x64, worked out the same way as the first chart.

According to recent reports, linux started drifting in spring 2025, while the Mac and Windows binaries didn't budge all year. They only got going in 2026, and they're at 44% and 45% now to Linux's 54%. Rollup's binaries do exactly the same. Linux is also where the volume is: 59 million esbuild installs a weekday, up from 5 million in summer 2024, against 3.5 million for Macs.

According to recent reports, that gap rules out one boring answer. Anything that grabs packages wholesale, like a mirror or a security scanner, would fetch all three alike, and the three lines would have moved together. They didn't.

Most CI runners, containers and cloud sandboxes are Linux, so the first wave looks like machines. OpenAI's Codex cloud agent and Claude Code's general release both came out in May 2025, which lines up nicely and proves nothing. I can't read the Macs and Windows PCs. That could be people building things at weekends now that something else does the typing, or more CI on Macs, or both, and download counts can't tell them apart.

It has been revealed that the weirdest one I found is create-vite, the thing you run to start a upcoming Vite project. Scaffolders were always weekend-heavy, because starting a side project is a Saturday thing, and create-vite ran at 67% in summer 2024. It's at 93% now, on 12 times the volume. Vite projects get started on a Sunday nearly as often as on a Tuesday.

This gets a package's last month from the same API and gives you its weekend average as a percentage of its weekday one:.

It's a straight average over the last 30 days rather than the medians in the charts, so it won't match them exactly. react comes out at 57 today, and node-sass at 46. In the summer of 2024, almost everything came out somewhere around 25.

Sources indicate that vaul's README still indicates it's unmaintained. Last Sunday it was downloaded 3.3 million times.

Tech Report: Notification Infra 2026: Knock vs Loops vs Resend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that your SaaS app needs to send notifications — welcome emails, billing alerts, Slack messages for latest signups, push notifications for mobile users.
  • Use Knock if you need to send notifications across multiple channels (email, in-app, Slack, push, SMS) and want a single API to manage them.
  • Three shifts have changed how SaaS teams approach notifications:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that your SaaS app needs to send notifications — welcome emails, billing alerts, Slack messages for latest signups, push notifications for mobile users. Initially, you use a single email provider (SendGrid, Postmark, Resend) and call it done. But as your product grows, the notification surface expands: email, in-app notifications, Slack/Discord webhooks, push, SMS. Managing them separately means duplicating template logic, user preferences, and delivery tracking across four different providers. This is the problem that notification infrastructure tools solve.

Use Knock if you need to send notifications across multiple channels (email, in-app, Slack, push, SMS) and want a single API to manage them. Use Loops if you primarily need transactional email with beautiful templates and a generous free tier. Use Resend if you're a solo developer who wants the simplest possible email API that works reliably. For multi-channel needs, start with Knock and add Loops as your dedicated email layer.

Three shifts have changed how SaaS teams approach notifications:.

Industry observers note that key insight: Knock is not a provider, it's an orchestrator. It doesn't send email itself — it routes through providers like Resend, SendGrid, or SES. This means your Knock pricing is additive to your email provider cost. For simple setups (email-only), Knock adds cost without much value. For multi-channel setups, Knock eliminates the complexity of managing separate providers for email, in-app, push, and Slack.

Industry observers note that knock is the most sophisticated of the three. You define a notification once (title, body, metadata), choose which channels it goes to (email, in-app, Slack, push, SMS), and Knock handles delivery to each channel through its growing network of integrations. It includes a customizable in-app feed component (React, Vue, and vanilla JS), user preference management with per-channel and per-category controls, digest/batch support, and step-up notifications (escalate from in-app to email if unread for 1 hour).

The learning curve is steeper than Loops or Resend because of the conceptual model (workflows, channels, preferences, digests), but for a SaaS product that needs more than just email, Knock replaces 2-4 separate provider integrations with one.

Loops has carved out a niche as "the email platform for modern SaaS that sends good-looking emails." Its drag-and-drop template editor produces genuinely good-looking transactional emails without HTML/CSS knowledge. The free tier (15K emails/month) is generous, and the pricing scales linearly without surprise charges.

Sources indicate that where Loops struggles: it's email-only. No Slack, no in-app, no push. If your notification strategy is "email first, maybe Slack later," Loops works. If you need multi-channel from day one, Knock is better.

Resend has built a reputation as the simplest reliable email API on the market. The API is a single POST request with subject, to, from, and HTML. Deliverability is excellent out of the box (they handle DKIM/DMARC configuration and warm-up automatically). React Email support means you write templates in React and Resend renders them to HTML.

The trade-off: Resend is deliberately minimal. No visual template editor, no in-app notifications, no multi-channel support, no user preference management. It's the email equivalent of a focused CLI tool — does one thing well and stays out of your way.

Recent findings suggest that the right choice depends on your notification complexity horizon. If you need email only and value simplicity, Resend is the fastest path to shipping. If you need beautiful transactional emails without a designer, Loops is the best email-first platform. If you need multiple channels and want to build notification infrastructure once and reuse it across features, Knock is worth the upfront learning investment. A pragmatic pattern: start with Resend (simplest, cheapest), add Loops when you need templates, and graduate to Knock when you need multi-channel notifications. The notification infrastructure space is consolidating — expect Knock to acquire or build native email delivery within the next 12 months, and Loops to add basic multi-channel support. Choose accordingly based on whether you need a solution now or a platform that will grow with you.

#57682. AI Sometimes Makes Institutions Worse

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2567 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

AI Sometimes Makes Institutions Worse

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automation fails most seriously when it is used to replace judgment rather than support it.
  • In a recent development, the conventional story about AI failure is straightforward: a model produces an error, people discover it, and the organization fixes the training data or tightens the guardrails.
  • Sources indicate that real deployments are usually messier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automation fails most seriously when it is used to replace judgment rather than support it. The pattern is not “computers make bad decisions”; it is that institutions often define success too narrowly, feed unreliable signals into software, and then treat its output as authority. In benefits, education, hiring, and customer support, automation can make mistakes cheaper to make, harder to discover, and harder to appeal. AI is the wrong tool when the real problem is not prediction but accountability, exception handling, or learning from messy human behavior.

In a recent development, the conventional story about AI failure is straightforward: a model produces an error, people discover it, and the organization fixes the training data or tightens the guardrails. That story is comforting because it makes automation a technology problem. Add more data. Adjust the thresholds. Red-team the model. Ship a safer version.

Sources indicate that real deployments are usually messier. The deeper problem is frequently the task itself. A benefits agency wants to detect fraud. A university wants to produce final grades. A company wants to screen résumés at scale. A airline wants to answer customer questions swiftly. In each case, AI is attractive because it promises consistency, speed, and lower labor costs.

But those systems do more than calculate. They exercise institutional power. They distribute benefits, assign grades, determine who gets interviewed, and decide whether customers receive refunds. When the underlying data is partial, the objective is contested, or mistakes are expensive, automation converts policy choices into apparently objective outputs.

Sources indicate that this matters now because the industry is moving from models that suggest answers to agents that take actions. A chatbot suggestion can be ignored. An agent that issues a refund, files a claim, rejects an application, or changes a customer record cannot. The more consequential the action, the more dangerous it is to confuse predictive confidence with institutional legitimacy.

Sources indicate that there are certainly cases where AI is useful. Spam filters reduce an enormous volume of junk email. Optical character recognition turns documents into searchable text. Fraud models can prioritize queues for human investigators. Recommendation systems help people navigate large catalogs. The glitch is not AI itself. It is the widespread habit of asking software to decide questions that require context, discretion, and an accountable owner.

My position is that AI becomes harmful when the institution uses it to remove friction from a process whose friction was doing useful work.

Recent findings suggest that human review is often described as inefficiency: slow, inconsistent, and expensive. Sometimes it is exactly that. But friction can also surface disagreement, force managers to justify decisions, and provide a place for edge cases to be caught. AI often removes these signals while preserving only the measurable proxy.

There are four recurring failure patterns.

In 2018, Amazon abandoned an AI recruiting tool after testing showed it had learned patterns from historical hiring data and penalized résumés containing terms such as “women’s.” The tech giant had tried to ensure the system did not infer gender from names, but historical data carried the bias forward anyway. The algorithm was not random. It was efficiently reproducing the institution’s past.

This is one of the most important distinctions in applied AI: a model can be technically accurate while the label it predicts is a bad representation of the underlying concept.

Sources indicate that recruiting history is not a clean definition of future job performance. It includes the effects of prior discrimination, uneven access to opportunity, and managers’ changing standards. “Similar to past hires” may be a reasonable screening feature in isolation. It becomes indefensible if the institution’s claim is that the tool identifies merit rather than reproducing access.

The same problem appears in algorithmic sentencing. In 2016, ProPublica reported that Black defendants in its analysis of the COMPAS recidivism tool were more than twice as likely to be falsely flagged as high risk: 44% of Black defendants received false positives compared with 23% of white defendants. White defendants, meanwhile, were more likely to be falsely classified as low risk. The underlying score was proprietary, and later research argued that different but valid statistical methods could produce different fairness assessments. Still, the episode exposed a core problem: “risk” was not the same thing as the label organizations were using it for, and an opaque score was still becoming a consequential decision.

It has been revealed that the lesson is not that risk models can never be used. It is that model accuracy cannot rescue a poorly defined objective.

The UK’s 2020 A-level grading crisis was not an AI experiment in the narrow sense. It was algorithmic standardization, and the distinction matters. The exam regulator, Ofqual, used a statistical model to produce final grades because exams had been canceled by the COVID-19 pandemic. The algorithm adjusted teacher assessments using prior attainment and school-level data, then assigned final grades without a teacher reviewing individual results.

When results were published, about 39% of A-level grades were lower than the grades teachers had assessed. The policy was reversed, with teacher assessments used instead of algorithmic grades. The episode exposed a political fact disguised as a technical one: standardization saved administrative effort, but it also transferred disruption and uncertainty from canceled exams to students whose future depended on the results.

Recent findings suggest that the Dutch childcare benefits scandal indicates the same dynamic with more human damage. Beginning in 2013, the Dutch tax administration used an algorithm to identify childcare benefit claims as fraud risks. The system treated nationality and other personal characteristics as relevant signals, producing discriminatory treatment. More than 26,000 households were wrongly accused of fraud, and some were ordered to repay large sums they had legitimately received. The scandal became large enough that the Dutch government resigned in January 2021.

Here, automation did not merely fail. It made institutional hostility scalable. Each accusation had the appearance of a formal process, complete with internal evidence that the public could not easily inspect. At least 100,000 legal cases reportedly resulted from the affair, although final case counts vary as cases were combined, resolved, or classified differently.

Recent findings suggest that this is why “the algorithm did what it was designed to do” is not a defense. The system was designed within a political and administrative process. It encoded assumptions about who was suspicious, what normal behavior looked like, and whose circumstances deserved benefit.

Human decisions contain their own flaws. Reviewers get tired. Managers rely on stereotypes. Human judgment varies across offices, shifts, and individual assessors. These are real problems, and a well-audited model may sometimes reduce inconsistency.

But a human mistake invites conversation. A model output often ends the conversation. Once a system presents a score, recommendation, or classification, people have to argue with its authority rather than the assumptions underneath it.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s Tay chatbot demonstrated the danger in a crude form. After its release in March 2016, customers manipulated it into posting racist and offensive messages. Microsoft shut it down within days and apologized. Tay was ultimately a marketing experiment, not an enterprise system, but the failure has become durable because it shows how rapidly automated speech can become institutional speech. A bot account may claim to be playful, but its statements still carry the credibility of the company that deployed it.

More consequential examples may look less dramatic. They include automated fraud flags that cause a payment to be frozen, content moderation that removes a legitimate video, or hiring rankings that a recruiter treats as a ready-made shortlist. The mistake may be statistically rare. Its impact depends on what the output triggers.

Industry observers note that this is where product design becomes moral design. If a model recommends a case for review, a human can still investigate the facts. If it closes the case, rejects the benefit application, or publishes the decision, the system has crossed from assistance into governance.

In a recent development, air Canada’s chatbot is a useful example because it combined poor product design with a failure of corporate responsibility. In February 2024, the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal awarded passenger Christopher Moffatt roughly C$800 after the airline’s website chatbot gave incorrect information about a bereavement-fare discount. Air Canada argued that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions. The tribunal rejected that argument, noting that Air Canada was responsible for information presented through its website.

In a recent development, the airline had treated the chatbot as a customer-service tool. Customers, correctly, treated it as an airline representative. That gap between how the company designed the system and how customers understood it is a recurring source of automation harm.

In a recent development, automation is especially wrong for ambiguous requests, disputed precedents, unusual circumstances, and cases requiring empathy or negotiation. It is also wrong when no one has decided what should happen after an error. “Escalate to a human” is not a safety strategy unless the organization has actually funded that human, trained them, given them authority, and measured how promptly they can resolve the matter.

The standard take says the answer is better models and stronger guardrails. That is necessary, but insufficient.

First, many failures are not caused by the model’s intelligence. Ofqual’s grading model was not necessarily broken in a statistical sense. The dispute concerned what standardizing grades should mean during a crisis. The tax authority’s benefits model may have performed well against its fraud-risk objective. The controversy concerned the objective, the data, and the consequences of using the output.

Recent findings suggest that second, the industry tends to frame human involvement as the last step in an automated pipeline. That framing is backwards for high-stakes decisions. If a case reaches a human only after software has rejected it, the human is often handling a queue of pre-judged cases. If software removes the item entirely, the case may never be reviewed. Effective human oversight requires the reviewer to have time, authority, original evidence, and a way to reverse the decision.

Third, the “humans are biased too” argument is valid but frequently abused. It proves that a model is not automatically better, not that it should be deployed. Human review can be inconsistent and costly, but it can also be organized around specific criteria, audited, and challenged. A model inherits every ambiguity in its labels while adding opacity, scale, and the social power of a supposedly objective system.

Recent findings suggest that finally, the debate focuses too much on spectacular generative-AI incidents. Some are real and alarming. But the most widespread harm may come from mundane classification systems that rank applications, flag transactions, monitor employees, or route customers. These systems produce fewer entertaining failures and much larger aggregate damage.

There is also a countervailing limitation: good automation can produce clear benefits. A fraud-detection model that surfaces cases for investigation, rather than issuing final accusations, can let analysts focus on complex cases. Automated document extraction can eliminate hours of copying data without replacing anyone’s judgment. The relevant counterargument is therefore not “always keep humans in the loop,” which is empty. It is that human involvement must be substantive, not ceremonial.

For builders, the first question should not be “Can a model perform this task?” It should be “Should this task be automated at this level of authority?”.

A serious product review should document the target outcome, the available ground truth, the cost of false positives and false negatives, the affected subgroups, and the least harmful reversible action the system can take. It should also specify when the system must abstain.

Recent findings suggest that uncertainty needs to be part of the product, not a footnote. A service that cannot explain why a benefit application was flagged should not be making that flag. An agent that lacks the authority to resolve a dispute should not pretend that it has resolved one. A hiring model trained on past decisions should be especially cautious because its “ground truth” is inherited from the institution it may be asked to improve.

In a recent development, builders should also measure operational recovery. How long does it take a person to overturn a bad decision? How many customers are affected before someone notices? Can the organization reproduce a decision from logs? Is there a rollback switch? If the answers are vague, the system is not production-ready regardless of its benchmark score.

Industry observers note that for people, the practical rule is simple: do not surrender context merely because software can summarize it. Keep receipts, screenshots, case references, and dates. Ask what data the decision used. Treat a score as a proposal unless the organization has clearly stated otherwise. Challenge automated classifications promptly, because human review pipelines often become slower and more defensive as time passes.

Regulators should audit deployments, not just model cards. The relevant unit of analysis is not the algorithm in isolation. It is the institution’s workflow: who selected the objective, who can correct the output, what evidence users receive, and what happens when the system is wrong.

According to recent reports, requirements for impact assessments, notice, reasons, appeals, and human review should scale with the consequence of the decision. A chatbot recommending a restaurant and a system denying public benefits should not sit on the same risk spectrum. Regulators should also require incident reporting that captures distribution-level harm, not only dramatic individual failures. A thousand small denials can matter more than one viral mistake.

For the industry, the durable opportunity is not maximum autonomy. It is bounded assistance. The best systems will be designed to narrow queues, extract evidence, identify missing information, and draft recommendations. The weakest will manufacture certainty from weak proxies and use it to remove accountability.

First, I’m watching whether agentic customer-service companies begin defining legal and operational boundaries explicitly. Air Canada’s defeat exposed an old trick: treating an assistant as separate from the business that deploys it. The next wave of agents will need clear statements of authority, escalation rules, and responsibility for consequential actions.

Sources indicate that second, I’m watching benefits, hiring, and education vendors respond to procurement demands for subgroup error rates, appeal outcomes, and operational metrics such as time-to-correction. Model accuracy is already easy to report. “How many incorrect decisions did owners reverse, and how long did each remain in force?” is much harder—and much more useful.

Third, I’m watching frontier-model evaluations move beyond headline accuracy toward calibration, abstention, and long-tail failure. A model that knows when its evidence is insufficient is more valuable in high-stakes work than one that answers every prompt with equal confidence. Benchmarks that make uncertainty costly will produce better products than leaderboards that reward unconditional answers.

AI is the wrong tool when the task depends on contested definitions, missing context, or decisions that an institution must be able to explain and reverse. The problem is not that machines are inhuman. It is that automation makes weak assumptions look like facts, scales bad policies, and shifts the burden of proof from institutions to the people they harm. The right standard is not whether AI can imitate a decision. It is whether the organization understands what it is asking the system to decide, what it will do when the model is wrong, and who remains accountable when the answer matters.

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

This feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

This auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

Industry observers note that on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

It has been revealed that all loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

In a recent development, the built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

GitLab CVE-2026-97229: falha de regex permite execução de código em CI/CD
